title: Mutation Testing
description: Measure test-suite strength by injecting small code mutations and checking which are caught — surviving mutants reveal tests that assert nothing meaningful.
body:
Mutation Testing

Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Coverage says a line ran; it does not say anyone would notice if it were wrong. Mutation testing flips the question: introduce small, mechanical changes to the code — flip a comparison, drop a call — and check whether the test suite fails. Surviving mutants are lines the suite does not actually defend, and each one is a concrete, fixable gap.

When to Use

Use when a suite has high coverage but defects still escape — release-critical libraries, parser cores, financial logic — and the question is whether the tests assert real behavior.

Do not run mutation testing over an entire large codebase at once; it multiplies suite runtime by the mutant count, so scope it to critical modules.

Inputs

Procedure
Select the scope deliberately — critical modules first — because every mutant costs a full suite run.
Apply mutations one at a time: small, mechanical edits such as flipping an operator, changing a constant, or removing a call.
Run the suite per mutant and record the result: killed, survived, or timed out.
Treat timeouts as kills only when the suite is deterministic; flaky suites make mutation results noise.
Group surviving mutants and convert each group into a missing assertion or a new test that kills it.
Re-run and compare the mutation score — the fraction killed — instead of trusting coverage alone.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Mutation testing modifies code in working directories and can, with careless tooling, leak mutants into builds. Run it in an isolated checkout, never commit mutated files, and gate CI on the original source with mutants applied only in ephemeral workspaces.

The mutmut mutation testing tool documentation (https://mutmut.readthedocs.io/).

title: Property Based Testing
description: Test executable invariants over generated inputs instead of fixed examples, then shrink failing cases toward minimal counterexamples that reproduce the defect with the least context.
body:
Property Based Testing

Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Example-based tests check the cases someone thought of; property-based tests state invariants and let a generator search the input domain for violations. When a generated case fails, shrinking reduces it toward the smallest reproducer, which becomes the bug report and a permanent regression test. This skill covers that loop — declare invariants, generate, shrink, repair — as a reviewable engineering procedure.

When to Use

Use when a function or service has a checkable invariant over a wide input space and hand-written examples cover only a thin slice of it.

Do not use for exact-output specifications or UI flows; deterministic example tests fit those better.

Inputs

Procedure
State each invariant as a predicate over generated inputs; an invariant that cannot be phrased as a predicate is a smell.
Define the input domain explicitly, including boundaries: empty, zero, negative, and maximum-shaped cases.
Run generated cases against each invariant and collect every failing input.
Shrink each failing input toward a minimal reproducer; the shrunk case is what gets reported.
Pin the shrunk counterexample as a permanent deterministic example test.
Repair the defect, re-run the full property, and only then remove any temporary filters.
Rotate seeds on a schedule; a fixed seed set forever is just a slow example suite.
Record which invariants ran; an unexercised invariant is untested behavior.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Property-based testing grants no authority to run generated inputs against production systems. Generators produce untrusted data: targets under test must be sandboxed, and shrinking must never reduce toward inputs that trigger real side effects.

title: Static Analysis
description: Find defects without executing code — dataflow, taint paths, and lint rules — triaging true positives from noise with a stated, documented rule inventory.
body:
Static Analysis

Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Static analysis reads code the way a reviewer with infinite patience would: every path, every assignment, every tainted flow from input to dangerous sink. Its problem is signal — tools over-report, and untriaged findings train teams to ignore them. This skill covers configuring analyzers, triaging output honestly, and maintaining a rule inventory that documents why each rule earns its noise.

When to Use

Use as a continuous gate on changed code and as a periodic deep pass — taint analysis on untrusted-input paths, security rules on everything that handles data.

Do not run analyzers in default configuration over legacy code and report thousands of findings at once; that output gets archived rather than acted on.

Inputs

Procedure
Configure a profile for the codebase: enabled rules, severities, and the reasoning that each noisy rule is worth its cost.
Analyze the whole program where the tool supports it — cross-function taint paths die at file scope.
Triage every finding against the baseline: confirm, waive with a reason, or fix now; never leave untriaged findings in the gate.
Distinguish findings by kind — real defect, style preference, false positive — and adjust rules to shrink the third category.
Feed confirmed security findings to the defect queue with the taint path attached, not just the line number.
Re-baseline after fixes: the baseline records what was consciously accepted, not what was ignored.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Static analysis is itself a security control, and its output is sensitive: a triaged findings list is a map of known weaknesses. Restrict access to findings, share waivers with the team that owns the code, and do not publish detailed weakness inventories for unfixed systems.

description: Emit logs as structured events — timestamp, level, ids, and measured fields — with stable schemas, correlation ids, and redaction rules instead of free-text lines.
body:
Structured Logging

Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A log line that only a human can parse is a cost center: it cannot be filtered, alerted on, or audited at scale. Structured logging emits events — a stable name, a level, a timestamp, and measured fields — with correlation ids that tie each event to the request or agent step that produced it, and redaction rules that keep sensitive values out of records by design.

When to Use

Use whenever more than one system or more than one day separates writing from reading — services, pipelines, agent frameworks — where logs must be filtered by field rather than grepped by hope.

Do not log raw payloads as fields; structure exists partly to make redaction enforceable.

Inputs

Procedure
Define the event vocabulary first — a stable event name per operation, with a documented field schema per event.
Include correlation ids in every event: request id, run id, step id, so a chain is reconstructable across systems.
Emit at the level that matches the reader: debug for development detail, info for operations, warning for degraded-but-serving, error for failures with an owner.
Redact by schema rather than by review: sensitive fields are masked or dropped at emit time, before any sink sees them.
Measure rather than narrate: durations, counts, and statuses as typed fields, with free text as a supplement rather than the record.
Log an error once with full context at the handling site, not re-logged at every layer of propagation.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Logs are among the most commonly exfiltrated artifacts: they outlive sessions, replicate to multiple sinks, and reach wide audiences. Enforce schema-level redaction, treat log systems as production data stores, and audit what event fields can carry before adding them.

title: Audience Analysis
description: Profile who will receive a message — their prior knowledge, stakes, and constraints — before deciding what to say and in what form to say it.
body:
Audience Analysis

Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Most failed communication was written before anyone asked who would read it. This skill front-loads that question: name the audience precisely, establish what they already know and what is at stake for them, and let those facts decide depth, order, and channel. The profile constrains the wording, not the truth — it changes how something is said, never whether the substance gets stated.

When to Use

Use before sending anything consequential to a group you cannot see — documentation, announcements, incident notices, decision requests.

Do not use the profile to stereotype individuals or to substitute imagined preferences for the purpose of the message; a profile guides wording, it does not license telling people only what they want to hear.

Inputs

Procedure
Name the audience precisely: "all users" is not an audience, while "first-time administrators configuring single sign-on" is.
Establish the baseline: what the reader already knows, so the message starts where they are rather than where the author wishes they were.
Establish the stakes: what changes for the reader if they act, and what changes if they do not.
Decide depth per segment — background, working detail, or decision summary — because one message cannot be all three at once.
Choose the channel and format each segment actually reads, and record constraints such as length limits or review requirements.
Revisit the profile when feedback arrives, because audiences drift and a stale profile misroutes everything built on it.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Audience analysis is a distribution decision, and distribution is a boundary: the segments a message will reach must feed directly into what it may contain, and no segment broader than the intended trust level of the content may be added as a recipient.

title: Feedback Delivery
description: Deliver critique so the recipient can act on it — observed behavior, concrete impact, and a specific request, separated from judgment of the person.
body:
Feedback Delivery

Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Feedback fails in two directions: it is so soft the recipient misses the point, or so blunt the recipient defends instead of acting. This skill holds the message to three separable parts — what was observed, what it caused, and what change is requested — and refuses to mix them with verdicts about the person. The test of good feedback is not how it feels in the moment; it is whether the next artifact observably changes.

When to Use

Use when reviewing work product — code, writing, analysis, performance — in written reviews or in conversation.

Do not use feedback structure to smuggle in verdicts about people, and do not deliver critique when either party is depleted; timing is part of the message.

Inputs

Procedure
Ground in observation: quote the artifact or name the behavior before interpreting it.
State impact concretely: what follows from the behavior, for whom, measurably where possible.
Make the request specific and checkable — name a change a future reader could verify happened.
Keep person and artifact separate: critique the work, never the character or motives of the worker.
Check receipt: ask what the recipient heard, and correct drift before it hardens into grievance.
Close the loop: record what was agreed, and revisit it after the next instance of the same work.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Review feedback can surface sensitive detail: findings about security flaws belong in channels scoped to the trust of the recipient, with exploitable specifics kept out of open threads until a fix or a disclosure decision is made.

title: Incident Communication
description: Write timely, structured incident updates — severity, impact, and a committed next-update time — so stakeholders stay informed while responders keep working.
body:
Incident Communication

Category: Communication | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

An incident produces two obligations at once: fix the thing, and tell the truth about it at a pace people can rely on. This skill separates narration from response — a designated owner handles the updates while responders respond — and gives each message a fixed shape: observed impact, current status, and when the next message lands. The cadence promise is the core mechanism: a stakeholder who knows the next update arrives in thirty minutes reads silence as work, not as abandonment.

When to Use

Use whenever an incident is visible to anyone beyond the responders — customers, leadership, partner teams — and from the first acknowledgement, not from the moment of diagnosis.

Do not let updates displace response work, and do not publish causal claims before evidence supports them; a stated unknown ages better than a wrong early diagnosis.

Inputs

Procedure
Send the first notice early: what is observably wrong, who is affected, and that response is underway.
Commit to a cadence and state it — the next update lands at a named time even if the only news is that nothing has changed.
Keep one authoritative channel; summaries posted elsewhere link to it rather than retell it.
Separate facts from hypothesis inside every message: label each statement as observed, inferred, or currently unknown.
Match depth to audience: leadership receives impact and decisions, responders receive technical detail, customers receive effect and remedy.
Close explicitly when the incident resolves — final impact, root-cause status, and where the postmortem will land.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Incident updates leak information under time pressure: state impact plainly, but keep credentials, internal hostnames, and customer identifiers out of widely-distributed notices; sensitive technical detail belongs in the restricted responder channel, and the public record should be written as if it will be quoted.

Meeting Notes

Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Meeting value leaks through unrecorded decisions and ownerless actions. This skill defines a note contract for live meetings: capture decisions with attribution and verbatim wording where it matters, convert actions into owner-task-date triplets, and keep open questions visible with a follow-up owner. The notes are the record; the transcript is only the input.

When to Use

Use when a live or asynchronous meeting produces decisions or actions that anyone must act on later.

Do not use for verbatim transcripts or archival records; capture and summarization skills fit those goals.

Inputs

Procedure
Record every participant and role before discussion starts; unattributable statements are flagged, not guessed.
Capture decisions with their speaker, the exact phrasing, and the point in the agenda where they were made.
Extract actions as owner, task, and due date; a missing owner is recorded as UNASSIGNED, never silently filled.
Keep open questions in their own list with a named follow-up owner and a next checkpoint.
Quote verbatim where wording matters; paraphrase only when the meaning is unambiguous.
Publish the structured notes in the same channel as the meeting so latecomers see the same record.
Reconcile actions against the previous meeting’s notes; uncompleted actions carry forward visibly.
Retain the notes under the organization’s retention policy; notes are records, not scratch space.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Taking notes grants no authority to speak for participants. Attributed statements must match what the participant actually said, and notes shared beyond the meeting must respect the organization’s information-handling rules. title: Negotiation
description: Prepare and conduct negotiations by mapping the interests behind stated positions, quantifying reservation values and alternatives, and trading on differences to reach agreements that hold.
body:
Negotiation

Category: Communication | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Negotiation is reaching agreement when parties' interests partly conflict. The reliable core is preparation: separating positions from interests, knowing your reservation value and best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA), and identifying differences that can be traded instead of split. This skill covers that preparation and the conduct of exchanges that produce precise, verifiable terms — without fabricating leverage or inventing concessions.

When to Use

Use when terms must be agreed with a party that has its own interests: scope and price discussions, vendor terms, resource allocation between teams.

Do not use it to manipulate or deceive a counterpart; commitments made must be within your actual mandate.

Inputs

Procedure
Convert each stated position into the interest behind it; list them in priority order.
Quantify the reservation value: the worst acceptable outcome, derived from constraints and BATNA, not from hope.
Inventory tradable differences: things cheap for you and valuable to them, and vice versa.
Propose packages across several issues rather than conceding issue by issue.
Test every emerging agreement against both sides' alternatives; an agreement worse than a party's BATNA will not hold.
Close with precise terms: who, what, when, and how verification happens.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

An agent negotiates only within an explicit mandate from its principal. Never commit beyond that scope, never share confidential information beyond what the mandate permits, and surface the walk-away recommendation instead of agreeing to terms outside the reservation envelope.

title: Plain Language Writing
description: Rewrite technical statements so a busy reader needs no extra context — short sentences, concrete nouns, active verbs, and no jargon left undefined.
body:
Plain Language Writing

Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Plain language is not simplified thinking; it is text that survives first contact with a reader who has no reason to reread it. This skill works mostly by subtraction: state the point in one sentence, prefer words the reader already owns, split sentences that carry more than one idea, and cut hedges until a claim stands alone. Terms of art survive only when they are load-bearing, and then they are defined on first use.

When to Use

Use for mixed or non-specialist audiences — documentation, summaries, status updates, user-facing messages — wherever the reader cannot be assumed to share the vocabulary of the author.

Do not strip precision that the audience needs; plain language is calibrated to its readers, and for a specialist audience the shared vocabulary is part of the clarity, not an obstacle to it.

Inputs

Procedure
Write the point in one sentence before touching the draft; if that sentence does not exist, the passage has no spine yet.
Replace each term of art with plain wording, or keep it and define it on first use when the term is load-bearing.
Split any sentence that carries more than one idea, and put the actor before the verb in each half.
Cut throat-clearing openings and stacked hedges; say the claim once and let it stand.
Pair every number with a reference point, because bare figures force the reader to supply the missing scale.
Reread as the target reader, and delete anything that survives only to comfort the author.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Plain text travels: writing for a broad audience multiplies the chance a passage is quoted out of context, so a rewrite must not widen disclosure — anything sensitive stays in documents scoped to the audience that may see it, and the plain version inherits the classification of its source.

Evidence

The PlainLanguage.gov guidelines (https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/).

title: API Pagination
description: Walk paged API result sets to completion — cursor or page parameters, per-request limits, and a terminal condition — without missing or double-processing records.
body:
API Pagination

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A paged response is a promise that the full list exists and a refusal to hand it over at once. This skill treats the pager as an explicit state machine: the request carries the continuation token, the response carries the next one, and iteration stops only when the API says it is finished. Rate limits are part of the traversal, not an error condition — a pager that ignores them will be right about the data and wrong about the budget.

When to Use

Use whenever an API returns lists with a cursor, page token, or offset parameter — directories, event logs, resource listings — and the task needs the complete set.

Do not fetch all pages when the task only needs a bounded prefix; a search that stops at the first match should not traverse the whole corpus.

Inputs

Procedure
Read the API contract for its pagination style — cursor, offset, or page token — before writing any loop.
Issue the first request with the largest page size the API allows, because fewer round trips is fewer chances to rate-limit.
Hand each record to the collector as its page arrives, rather than accumulating every page in memory.
Persist the continuation token between requests, and treat an absent or null token as the terminal condition — never a missing key.
Respect the rate limit: back off when the API says so, and prefer the retry-after guidance over a fixed sleep when it is offered.
Record the traversal outcome — pages fetched, records seen, terminal reason — so an incomplete walk is detectable after the fact.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Continuation tokens are credentials for data position: they can leak record ranges and query context when logged or shared, so treat them as sensitive in logs, and scope every traversal to the caller whose credentials opened it — a walk must never resume under a different principal.

Evidence

title: API Version Pinning
description: Pin every external API to a specific, recorded version — and upgrade as a deliberate, tested change — so upstream evolution never rewrites behavior silently.
body:
API Version Pinning

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

An unpinned API call is a bet on someone else's release calendar. This skill removes the bet: each external dependency is pinned to a concrete version in configuration, the pin is visible in code review, and upgrades happen as deliberate changes with a diff, a changelog read, and a test pass. Pinning goes further than a version number where the provider allows it — dated pins and versioned endpoints record the wire behavior the tests actually exercised.

When to Use

Use for every external API integration that reaches production, and pin in configuration rather than in a dependency default.

Do not pin so hard that upgrades never happen; an integration left on an unsupported version is a slower, quieter failure mode.

Inputs

Procedure
Record the pin in configuration, not in a lockfile default or a floating latest, so it appears in review and in audits.
Read the provider versioning model — dated pins, endpoint versions, deprecation windows — and record the model beside the pin.
Subscribe to change: watch the changelog or deprecation feed for the pinned version, and treat deprecation notices as scheduled work.
Upgrade deliberately: new pin, changelog diff read, integration tests run, and the change shipped as its own reviewable commit.
Roll back the pin, not the code, when an upgrade misbehaves — the pin is the smallest reversible unit.
Audit pins periodically: a pin on an unsupported version is a defect even while everything still works.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Version pins interact with trust: upgrading an API client changes what is sent and to whom, so pin changes deserve security review like any dependency change, and a pin must never be loosened to make an unrelated integration problem go away.

title: Streaming Tool Output
description: Consume tool output as it arrives — newline-delimited chunks, incremental parsers, bounded buffers — so long-running results become usable before they finish.
body:
Streaming Tool Output

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Some tool calls are streams pretending to be calls: search results that arrive page by page, logs that emit lines for minutes, models that produce tokens before the sentence is done. This skill treats the output as a sequence with a protocol — a delimiter or an event frame — and consumes it incrementally: parse what has arrived, hold a bounded remainder for the incomplete tail, and surface progress to whoever is waiting. The alternative is buffering everything, which turns a long result into a long silence followed by a large object.

When to Use

Use for long-running or high-volume tool output — event streams, incremental search, anything that delivers value before completion.

Do not add streaming machinery to short, fast calls; a buffered read of a small response is simpler and equally correct.

Inputs

Procedure
Fix the protocol first: know what delimits a record — a newline, a frame header, a terminator — before reading a byte.
Read incrementally and split on the delimiter, keeping the incomplete tail in a buffer rather than discarding it.
Dispatch each complete record to the handler immediately, so downstream work overlaps with the remaining stream.
Bound the buffer: a tail that grows past its limit is a protocol violation, and streaming must fail loudly, not allocate quietly.
Surface progress — records seen, bytes read — so a slow stream is observable while it runs.
Handle terminal conditions distinctly: end-of-stream, error frame, and cancellation are different events and must close differently.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Streamed output bypasses the size checks that whole responses get: incremental data must still be validated per record at the boundary, and progress events must not leak record contents into logs where whole payloads would never be allowed.

Evidence

This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references:
The JSON Lines format specification site (https://jsonlines.org/).
Wikipedia's overview of stream processing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_processing).

body:
Tool Output Validation

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A tool result is untrusted input with a confident tone: it arrives as a string, a dict, or a truncated fragment, and whatever shape it claims is a claim. This skill moves the checking to the boundary: each expected output is declared as a schema, each result is validated on arrival, and a failure is reported as a structured error with the offending path — not smuggled into the conversation for the caller to misread. Validation failures are normal control flow, not exceptions to silence.

When to Use

Use whenever a tool result feeds decisions — structured data, numeric values, identifiers — and especially when results come from external services outside your control.

Do not validate ad hoc fields nobody consumes; a schema that checks everything protects nothing in particular and costs every call.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare the schema for what the result must contain — required fields, types, and bounds — before calling the tool.
Validate on arrival: check presence first, then types, then value constraints such as ranges or enum membership.
Collect every violation with its path rather than failing on the first, so one pass describes the whole gap.
Route failures by policy: reject the result, attempt a bounded repair, or re-request once with a corrected call.
Never stringify a failed result into the reasoning stream; a rejected result enters as an error record with its path and reason.
Keep the schema under version control beside the tool integration, and bump it when the upstream contract changes.

title: Tool Result Caching
description: Reuse identical tool calls that already succeeded — keyed by operation and arguments — so repeat work costs a lookup instead of another remote round trip.
body:
Tool Result Caching

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Every tool call that returns the same answer for the same arguments is a cache wearing a network costume. This skill makes that explicit: a deterministic operation gets a cache key built from its identity and its arguments, responses are stored with a time-to-live and a staleness policy, and a hit must be marked as cached so downstream consumers know what they are reading. The discipline is deciding which calls are cacheable — deterministic and side-effect-free — before caching anything.

When to Use

Use for deterministic, read-only calls whose arguments repeat across a session or pipeline — enrichment lookups, reference data fetches, idempotent reads.

Do not cache calls whose results depend on hidden state, side effects, wall-clock time, or caller identity, and do not let a cache silently answer after the underlying data contract changes underneath it.

Inputs

Procedure
Confirm the operation is deterministic and side-effect-free; anything with hidden state is disqualified before a key is built.
Build the cache key from the operation identity and the full, normalized argument set, so two calls that differ only in formatting still share an entry.
Store the response with its time-to-live and the timestamp of the fetch, not the timestamp of the read.
On a hit, return the cached value marked as cached, with its original fetch time, so consumers can reason about staleness.
On expiry, refetch — or serve stale while refreshing when the policy allows — and record the miss rate per operation.
Invalidate by key when the underlying data is known to change, and treat a change in the data contract as a full invalidation.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

A cache is a copy of data outside its origin's access control: cache stores inherit the sensitivity of what they hold, so entries holding user-scoped or restricted data must be keyed to the caller's scope and evicted on scope change, never shared across principals.

title: Tool Schema Design
description: Design LLM tool schemas with disciplined names, bounded parameters, enumerated options, and structured errors so model calls stay valid, predictable, and cheap to validate.
body:
Tool Schema Design

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A tool schema is the contract between a model and an execution surface, and most tool failures are schema failures: vague names, unbounded numbers, free text where an enum fits, and error shapes nobody planned. This skill defines the design contract: name tools after their effects, bound every parameter, prefer closed value sets, reject unknown keys, and return structured errors the caller can branch on.

When to Use

Use when defining or revising an LLM-callable tool so that model errors become invalid calls instead of wrong effects.

Do not use for human-facing CLI design or internal library APIs; those audiences read documentation instead of schemas.

Inputs

Procedure
Name each tool after the effect it performs, verb first; a schema named after its data invites misuse.
Give every parameter a type, a description, and where possible a bound; unbounded parameters are rejections in waiting.
Prefer closed enums over free text wherever the value space is known.
Mark required parameters explicitly and document what omitting an optional one means.
Reject unknown keys; permissive parsing lets hallucinated parameters reach execution.
Return errors as structured payloads with a stable code, a human-readable message, and a retryability flag.
Validate calls against the schema before execution; a call that fails validation never reaches the effect.
Version the schema; breaking changes take a new tool name, not a silent redefinition.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Designing a tool schema grants no execution authority. Schemas bound what a call may contain, not what it may do: the execution surface still enforces its own permission checks, rate limits, and audit logging. Error messages must never echo credentials or internal paths.

description: Establish and maintain WebSocket sessions with framing-correct message handling, heartbeat keepalives, reconnect with bounded backoff, and explicit close-code interpretation.
body:
WebSocket Communication

Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

The WebSocket protocol upgrades an HTTP connection into a long-lived, bidirectional message channel. Unlike a single HTTP call, a session lives for minutes or hours, so the real engineering is in staying healthy: heartbeats, bounded reconnect backoff, close-code interpretation, and queues that do not grow without limit.

When to Use

Use when the remote endpoint provides a WebSocket API and the workload is genuinely streaming or bidirectional: live feeds, telemetry, interactive tool protocols.

Prefer ordinary HTTP for one-shot request/response; a session adds failure modes, not value.

Inputs

Procedure
Open the handshake and validate the negotiated subprotocol against the one you expect.
Route incoming frames through handlers; answer server pings automatically.
Send heartbeats on the configured cadence and treat a missed pong as a dead session, not a busy one.
On abnormal close, reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter; cap the delay and the total retry budget.
Interpret close codes precisely: 1000 is a normal close with no retry, 1006 is abnormal (no close frame), 1011 is a server error that may not be retryable.
Bound both send and receive queues; drop or fail explicitly rather than buffering without limit.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Use  everywhere outside localhost;  is plaintext. Validate the Origin on the server side, treat every inbound frame as untrusted input, and never reconnect with credentials that the endpoint should no longer hold.

title: Audio Diarization
description: Segment an audio stream into who-spoke-when turns from frame-level acoustic evidence with deterministic boundary rules so speaker attribution yields explicit, testable segments.
body:
Audio Diarization

Category: Multimodal | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Speaker attribution is only as trustworthy as its segment boundaries. This skill builds diarization as a rule-bound pipeline: acoustic frames carry a speaker label, consecutive same-label frames merge into turns, and every turn records its speaker, start, and end. The merge rules are deterministic so the same frame sequence always produces the same turn list. Acoustic labeling itself is delegated to a classifier; this skill governs the segmentation contract.

When to Use

Use when a transcript or analysis needs per-speaker attribution — meeting minutes, call analytics, or speaker-indexed search — and the output must be a reviewable turn list rather than a black-box label.

Do not use for raw transcription without speakers; apply the audio transcription skill instead, and diarize its alignment if per-speaker turns are needed.

Inputs

Procedure
Require frames to be sorted by start time before merging; unsorted input is rejected.
Merge a frame into the previous turn only when speaker labels match and boundaries are contiguous.
Start a new turn on any label change, gap, or boundary discontinuity; never merge across gaps.
Apply the minimum-turn rule after merging, dropping turns shorter than the declared floor.
Record each turn as (speaker, start, end) with an identifier stable across runs.
Expose a coverage metric: total speech time minus turn gaps, so silent regions are visible.
Treat classifier labels as evidence, not truth: keep the label confidence alongside each turn when available.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Diarization output identifies who spoke when; treat it as personal data. It grants no authority to act on speakers and must respect the retention and consent rules of the source audio in every downstream store.

description: Blend multiple PCM audio tracks under explicit gain envelopes with sample-accurate summation, hard clipping bounds, and a measured output peak so a mix is reproducible and cannot silently exceed the output range.
body:
Audio Mixing

Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Mixing becomes destructive the moment gain is improvised: summed samples clip, quiet tracks get buried, and the result varies run to run. This skill treats a mix as an explicit contract — per-track gains, optional timed envelopes, a declared clip limit, and a measured peak — so the output is byte-reproducible from its inputs. It operates on in-memory PCM sample lists; codec-level or streaming mixdowns are out of scope.

When to Use

Use when combining two or more recorded or synthesized mono PCM tracks into one output track where loudness behavior and clipping must be decided by policy rather than by accident.

Do not use for real-time streaming mixdowns or codec-domain processing; apply this contract after decoding, on sample data.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare every track gain and the clip limit before the first sample is summed; mixing with undeclared gains is rejected.
Verify all tracks share a sample rate and channel layout; resample or reject before mixing, never inside it.
Apply each track’s gain (and optional timed envelope) sample by sample, in a fixed track order.
Sum tracks sample-accurately in integer domain so the result is identical across runs and platforms.
Clip each summed sample to the declared limit and count clipped samples as a quality signal.
Measure the output peak after mixing; an unmeasured mix cannot be compared or improved.
Record the gain set, envelope, clip count, and peak alongside the output so the mix is reproducible.
Re-mix rather than normalize after the fact when the clip count is nonzero; clipping already destroyed information.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Mixing grants no authority over source recordings. Source material keeps its license and consent state; a mix does not launder restricted audio into usable output. Output loudness is a technical measurement, not a safety claim.

title: Image Resizing
description: Compute contain and cover resize boxes with integer arithmetic, explicit rounding, and declared upscale policy so scaled pixel targets are deterministic across runtimes.
body:
Image Resizing

Category: Multimodal | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

“Scale to fit” hides two different contracts: contain fits the whole image inside a box with letterboxing, cover fills the box and crops the overflow. This skill computes both as pure integer math with declared rounding and upscale rules, so every runtime derives the same target box from the same inputs. Resampling filters and color management are out of scope; this is the geometry contract that runs before them.

When to Use

Use when a fixed display box must receive images of arbitrary aspect ratio and the output box — letterboxed, cropped, or bounded — must be computed exactly.

Do not use for art-directed aspect changes; creative crop choices belong to image editing, not to mechanical geometry.

Inputs

Procedure
Reject non-positive dimensions or box before computing.
Compute contain as the minimum scale that fits both sides, never exceeding the box on either axis.
Compute cover as the maximum scale that fills both sides, at least as large as the box on either axis.
Floor results to integer pixels with one documented rounding rule applied to both axes.
Apply the upscale policy: contain never exceeds the source size unless enlargement is declared; cover enlarges only as required to fill.
Return the box with the effective scale and the crop offsets for cover, so the caller can apply them mechanically.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Resizing grants no authority over source media and removes no protection: an access-controlled image stays access-controlled at every derived size, and metadata stripping is a separate decision that must be made explicitly.

Wikipedia’s overview of image scaling algorithms (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_scaling).

title: Image Super-Resolution
description: Upscale low-resolution images with model-based super-resolution while bounding hallucinated detail, preserving identity-critical features, and labeling the synthesized output as reconstruction.
body:
Image Super-Resolution

Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Super-resolution uses a learned model to upscale an image beyond its pixel count. The model invents plausible high-frequency detail; it does not recover what was truly there. This skill covers applying SR appropriately, inspecting the output for hallucinated structure, and keeping the output labeled as a reconstruction — never as recovered evidence.

When to Use

Use for restoring legacy assets, enlarging crops for human viewing, and cleaning up downscaled media where plausibility is the goal.

Do not use SR output for identification, forensics, medical reading, or any decision where invented detail could be mistaken for captured fact.

Inputs

Procedure
Confirm the use case permits synthesized detail; refuse evidentiary use up front.
Select the model variant matching the content type; text and faces need the strictest handling.
Run SR at a power-of-two scale; larger factors by chained passes, not one extreme pass.
Inspect the output for hallucination signatures: invented text glyphs, warped faces, repeated window or brick patterns.
Keep the original untouched alongside the output; never overwrite the source.
Record in metadata that the image is model-upscaled, with model and scale named.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Super-resolution output is synthesized imagery. It must be labeled as such, must not feed identification or forensic pipelines, and must not be presented in a way that implies detail the sensor never captured.

Evidence

The Real-ESRGAN image restoration project (https://github.com/xinntao/Real-ESRGAN).
The realesrgan Python package (https://pypi.org/project/realesrgan/).

title: Perceptual Image Hashing
description: Compute average-hash fingerprints from downsampled grayscale data and compare them by Hamming distance so near-duplicate images are detected without byte equality.
body:
Perceptual Image Hashing

Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Byte hashes cannot recognize the same picture after a resize or re-encode. A perceptual hash captures visual structure: downsample to a fixed grid, threshold each cell against the grid mean, and pack the bits into a fixed-width fingerprint. Two images then compare by Hamming distance, and a declared threshold turns that distance into a duplicate decision. Face or semantic similarity is out of scope; this is structural near-duplicate detection.

When to Use

Use when a corpus must be deduplicated against resizes, crops, and re-encodes, and the decision must be explainable as a measured distance against a declared threshold.

Do not use for semantic matching — different scenes with similar histograms compare equal; use classification or embedding retrieval for meaning-level search.

Inputs

Procedure
Downsample every image to the same fixed grayscale grid before hashing; grid mismatch makes hashes incomparable.
Compute the grid mean and threshold every cell to one bit, using a strict greater-than comparison.
Pack the bits in row-major order into a fixed-width integer fingerprint.
Compare fingerprints by Hamming distance — popcount of the XOR — never by string similarity.
Apply the declared duplicate threshold and record the distance, not just the verdict.
Treat dark, flat, or synthetic grids as unhashable noise: their bits carry no structure and produce false matches.
Never edit images to force a match; if distances sit at the threshold, collect more evidence instead.

Security and Authority Boundary

Perceptual hashes are derived features of their source images; they inherit every access restriction of the source. A hash that survives deletion of the original can still identify it, so retention policy must cover hashes too.

Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

A caption file is a format contract: cue timestamps must be ordered, non-overlapping, and formatted to the millisecond, or players drop or smear cues. Format every timestamp as HH:MM:SS.mmm computed from seconds with integer millisecond rounding.
Reject any segment whose end precedes or equals its start; malformed timing never reaches the output.
Detect overlaps between consecutive cues and fail closed instead of silently emitting both.

body:
Thumbnail Generation

Category: Multimodal | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A thumbnail pipeline needs one deterministic answer per input: given a source size and a bound, what target box does every runtime agree on? This skill defines that answer with integer math — scale by the limiting side, floor to whole pixels, never upscale past the bound — so galleries and indexes render identical sizes everywhere. Pixel resampling quality is out of scope; this is the sizing contract.

When to Use

Use when generating preview images for galleries, feeds, or search results where the target box must be computed, not guessed, and must match across implementations.

Do not use for art-directed crops; creative sizing belongs to image editing, not to this mechanical contract.

Inputs

Procedure
Reject non-positive width, height, or maxside before any math runs.
Compute the scale as the minimum of maxside/width, maxside/height, and 1 when upscaling is disabled.
Apply the scale to both dimensions and floor to whole pixels, flooring identically in every implementation.
Clamp each result to at least one pixel so degenerate inputs never yield an empty box.
Return the box together with the computed scale so callers can verify the bound was respected.
Keep the operation pure: same inputs, same box, no environment state.

title: Agent Checkpointing
description: Persist an agent run as resumable checkpoints — state, memory, pending actions — so a failure or restart continues from a recorded point instead of from scratch.
body:
Agent Checkpointing

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A long agent run that cannot resume is a long agent run that will eventually be repeated. This skill treats the run as a sequence of durable states: after each completed step, the run writes a checkpoint — conversation state, working memory, pending tool calls — and a restart restores the latest one before doing anything else. The design question is granularity: checkpoints cost writes, and restarts cost rework, so the checkpoint cadence is chosen by what re-execution is actually allowed to cost.

When to Use

Use for long-running or stateful agent work — multi-step plans, sessions holding tool state, pipelines vulnerable to timeout or restart.

Do not checkpoint every intermediate token of fast, cheap runs; when re-execution costs less than persistence, the checkpoint is pure overhead.

Inputs

Procedure
Choose the checkpoint unit — step, tool call, or plan stage — based on what re-execution of that unit is allowed to cost.
Serialize complete state, not deltas alone: a checkpoint that needs every prior checkpoint to restore is a chain, not a checkpoint.
Write the checkpoint atomically, so a crash mid-write leaves the previous checkpoint intact rather than a torn one.
On restart, restore the latest checkpoint first and reconcile with reality — replay tool side effects only where the tool contract allows it.
Version the checkpoint schema; a restored run must refuse to continue on a state format it cannot fully interpret.
Prune old checkpoints on a retention rule, and record the retention decision so the pruning is explainable later.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

A checkpoint is a complete, portable copy of agent state — credentials in working memory get persisted with it, so checkpoints must inherit the encryption and access scope of the run itself, and the pruning policy must respect data-retention obligations, not just disk budgets.

title: Agent Failure Taxonomy
description: Classify agent failures into a shared, evidence-based taxonomy — planning, retrieval, reasoning, execution, environment — so fixes land at the right layer.
body:
Agent Failure Taxonomy

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Agents fail in characteristic ways, and a fix aimed at the wrong layer is a fix that did not happen. This skill gives the failures names: a plan that never fit the goal, retrieval that brought back wrong evidence, reasoning that misjoined what it had, execution that fumbled a working plan, environment that changed under the run. Classification comes from traces — where the first wrong step appears — and the taxonomy pays for itself by making postmortems comparable across incidents instead of anecdotal.

When to Use

Use when reviewing a failed agent run — incident triage, postmortem, quality review — before anyone decides what to change.

Do not skip classification and jump to the most recent failure; without a layer verdict, fixes become folklore and the same class recurs.

Inputs

Procedure
Reconstruct the run from its trace: what was asked, what was retrieved, what was decided, what was executed.
Locate the first wrong step — the earliest point where the run departed from a path that could still reach the goal.
Classify by layer: planning, retrieval, reasoning, execution, or environment, using the criteria of the taxonomy rather than intuition.
Distinguish root cause from symptom: a wrong answer is a symptom; the layer that injected the error is the cause.
Record the classification with its evidence — the trace excerpt that supports it — so the verdict is reviewable.
Aggregate over incidents: recurrence by class is the signal that directs where the next fix budget goes.

Outputs

Failure traces contain the data the run touched, including anything sensitive it retrieved or produced: postmortems and classification records must redact secrets at capture time, because a taxonomy entry quoting a credential is a leak with good documentation.

title: Approval Gates
description: Pause an agent run at defined checkpoints and route the pending action to a human decision, so consequential steps execute only after an explicit approval.
body:
Approval Gates

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Autonomy is a budget, not a binary. This skill spends it deliberately: the run defines which action classes are safe to execute directly, which require a human decision before they commit, and what information the human needs to decide. A gate is a structured pause — the agent stops, presents the action and its context, and waits; the decision is recorded with the action it authorized, so the audit trail says who allowed what, not just what ran.

When to Use

Use for irreversible or consequential actions — payments, deletions, production changes, external commitments — and for action classes whose blast radius exceeds a configured threshold.

Do not gate trivial, reversible steps; an approval process that fires a hundred times a day trains its approvers to click through without reading.

Inputs

Procedure
Classify actions up front: which execute without a gate, which need a human, and which are refused outright regardless of approval.
Define the gate payload before the run starts — action, arguments, predicted effect, and rollback path — so the pause presents a decision, not a mystery.
Stop cleanly: the agent suspends at the gate, persists the pending action, and surfaces the decision request to the designated approver.
Record the verdict with its provenance — who decided, when, and on what evidence — attached to the action it authorized.
Execute the approved action exactly as presented; a modified action re-enters the gate rather than riding an old approval.
Feed rejections back into policy: repeated refusals of the same action class mean the classification, not the human, is wrong.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

The gate record is an authority artifact: approvals must bind to the exact action hash and the identity of the approver, and gate logs deserve the same integrity protection as audit logs — an attacker who can forge either owns the blast radius of the agent.

Evidence

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework overview (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

title: Bounded Exploration
description: Spend a fixed exploration budget — trials, depth, wall time — on search and self-play style wandering, then commit to the best option found within the bound.
body:
Bounded Exploration

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Exploration without a budget is wandering with good intentions. This skill makes the budget explicit: a number of trials, a depth limit, a deadline, and a stopping rule that ends the search when the bound is hit or the returns flatten. The point is not that exploration is bad — it is that unbounded exploration defers commitment forever, and the commitment is where the value is. After the budget is spent, the agent stops comparing and starts using what it found.

When to Use

Use when an agent must search a large option space — candidate strategies, tool combinations, plan variants — under real cost or time constraints.

Do not spend exploration budget on cheap, well-understood decisions with an obvious best answer; explore where ignorance is real and the cost of being wrong is high.

Inputs

Procedure
Fix the budget before starting: trial count, depth limit, and deadline, written down so the run cannot renegotiate with itself.
Define the reward or quality signal before exploring; a search without a scoring function is a random walk with commentary.
Explore in rounds, keeping the best-so-far option at every round so the budget can end at any moment with something usable.
Track returns per round: when additional trials stop improving the best score, apply the stopping rule and keep the leftover budget.
Commit to the best option found within the bound, and record it with its score and the exploration that produced it.
Defer regret to calibration: revisit the budget size against outcomes over time, rather than restarting exploration on a single miss.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Exploration that invokes real tools spends real authority: an exploring agent must run under the same least-privilege scope as execution, and its trial actions must be recorded like any other — a search that can execute must never leave the audit log emptier than a commit would.

!Dependency Status

Chain of Thought (CoT)

Description

Forces the model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer. Pure prompting — no tools, no extra calls. On multi-step arithmetic, logic, and constrained planning, well-applied CoT typically lifts accuracy by 5–25 points on frontier models, and far more on smaller ones.

When to Use
The problem decomposes naturally into sequential steps (math, multi-fact reasoning, constrained planning).
Latency is acceptable (CoT roughly doubles output tokens).
You don't need the model to call external tools — for those, use ReAct.

Inputs / Outputs

Plan rigidity: executing a stale task list after the environment or goal changes; replanning must be triggered by explicit failure or change signals, not only by exhaustion of the list.

title: Prompt Caching
description: Order prompts so stable content forms a cacheable prefix, place cache breakpoints deliberately, and measure the achieved hit rate instead of assuming caching pays for itself.
body:
Prompt Caching

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Prompt caching only pays when the stable content is ordered first and the volatile content last, and it only keeps paying while someone measures the hit rate. This skill defines the ordering contract, breakpoint placement, and the measurement loop that decides whether caching is worth its constraints for a given workload.

When to Use

Use when an agent workload sends a large stable prefix every turn and the provider prices cached input below fresh input.

Do not use for single-shot prompts or workloads where the prefix changes every turn; caching adds constraints without return.

Inputs

Procedure
Order the prompt so the stablest content comes first: system text, then tool definitions, then history.
Place the volatile user request strictly last; anything after it cannot be cached on the next turn.
Declare cache breakpoints at the boundaries between stability tiers, not at arbitrary token counts.
Estimate cost with the cached and fresh prices before rollout; an unmeasured saving is an assumed one.
Measure the achieved hit rate over real turns, not synthetic ones.
Re-measure whenever system text or tool definitions change; a prefix change invalidates the cache at that breakpoint.
Keep the prefix genuinely stable; mostly stable content pays the fresh price every turn.
Report cached and non-cached cost separately in the budget so the saving is auditable.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Caching prompt content grants no authority to relax data handling. Cached segments may persist on the provider side beyond the request; content subject to retention or confidentiality limits must not be placed in cacheable positions without an explicit policy decision.

Evidence

This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references:
Anthropic’s Messages API reference covering prompt caching through the cache_control field (https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/messages).
OpenAI’s prompt caching documentation (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-caching).

title: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description: Ground generation with retrieved external context by separating ingestion, retrieval, context assembly, generation, and source attribution, with explicit handling for weak or conflicting retrieval.
body:
RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Description

RAG separates knowledge retrieval from language generation. The system retrieves relevant source material at query time, supplies that material to the generator, and preserves source references so the answer can be inspected.

RAG is a grounding architecture, not a guarantee against hallucination.

Pipeline

Inputs / Outputs

Runnable Example

This deterministic example uses lexical retrieval instead of pseudo-random vectors. It demonstrates the retrieval boundary without pretending to be a production embedding system.

Retrieval Design
Preserve stable document IDs and source locations.
Chunk according to document structure rather than arbitrary token counts alone.
Apply authorization, tenant, language, and document-type filters where required.
Keep retrieved context bounded.
Treat lexical, dense, hybrid, and reranked retrieval as separate components with independently measurable behavior.
Do not treat a retrieval score as a probability of correctness.
When sources conflict, expose the conflict instead of selecting one silently.

Generation Contract

A generator should receive the query, bounded retrieved context, source identifiers, and explicit instructions for missing or conflicting evidence.

Validate that every cited source identifier was actually retrieved. Citation presence alone does not prove support for the underlying claim.

Failure Modes

Evaluation

Measure retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval can use recall@k, precision@k, or ranking metrics against a fixed evaluation set. Generation should separately assess factual support, citation correctness, refusal behavior, and completeness.

Do not infer production readiness from a single benchmark.

Evidence
Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
LangChain retrieval concepts: https://python.langchain.com/docs/concepts/retrieval/

Evidence status: references support the architecture and evaluation concepts. No performance ranking or production-readiness claim is made.

!Dependency Status

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting)

Description

ReAct interleaves Thought (model reasoning), Action (a tool call), and Observation (the tool's return value) inside a single loop. The model picks the next tool based on what it has learned so far and stops when it can answer. It is the simplest working architecture for tool-using agents and the foundation that more elaborate patterns (Plan-and-Execute, LATS, Tool-Use Loop) build on.

When to Use
The task needs external information or actions (search, DB query, API call) — pure CoT is not enough.
You want a single tool-using loop that's easy to debug and inexpensive.
You can tolerate 5–15 model calls per task; for sub-second latency, prefer direct tool calls without the loop.

title: Skill Quality Evaluation
description: Evaluate a skill or skill package against measurable quality dimensions - description fidelity, instruction actionability, runnable example validity, failure-mode coverage, and evidence strength - and produce a scored, reproducible verdict before the skill is trusted, installed, or published.
body:
Skill Quality Evaluation

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Skill quality evaluation turns "is this skill good?" into a reproducible inspection with named dimensions and an explicit verdict. It scores a candidate skill against measurable quality dimensions - description fidelity, instruction actionability, runnable-example validity, failure-mode coverage, and evidence strength - and records the findings, so trusting, installing, publishing, or rejecting a skill is a documented decision instead of an impression.

This skill is intended for agent runtimes, registries, and maintainers who must decide whether a skill is fit to use or publish. It does not replace security auditing, benchmark execution, or human review; it complements them.

When to Use

Use when a skill is about to be installed, published, promoted, or relied on, and no current quality verdict exists for its version.

Do not use this as a substitute for a security audit of untrusted packages, or as proof that a skill works; a passing quality score is not evidence of runtime effectiveness.

Inputs

Evaluation Procedure
Inventory the artifact: frontmatter, body, runnable example, and any bundled package files.
Check description fidelity: does the declared description match what the body actually instructs?
Check instruction actionability: are the instructions specific and verifiable, or vague aspiration?
Check the runnable example: does it run, is it deterministic where determinism is claimed, and does it exercise the core contract?
Check failure-mode coverage: are realistic failure modes named with causes and mitigations?
Check evidence strength: which claims carry dated, traceable evidence, and which are unevidenced?
Score each dimension with the agreed weights and compute the weighted total.
Apply the verdict policy to produce PASS, NEEDS-WORK, or FAIL with explicit blockers.
Record dimension scores, findings, and the verdict as a dated review artifact.
Re-evaluate when the skill changes version or when new contrary evidence appears.

Outputs

Decision Contract

A valid evaluation must answer all of these questions:
Which dimensions were scored, with what weights and thresholds?
Does the description match the instructions?
Is the example runnable and representative?
Which failure modes are covered and which are missing?
Which claims carry dated evidence and which do not?
What findings block a PASS verdict?
What change or evidence would reopen the verdict?

A skill must not be marked high-quality solely because it is popular, long, or recently updated.

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Quality evaluation grants no permissions and does not execute the skill under test beyond its own runnable example in a controlled environment. Untrusted skills must additionally pass a dedicated security audit before installation or execution.

High-impact publication or installation decisions remain subject to the governing approval controls of the consuming runtime.

Evidence

This skill is motivated by dated public ecosystem evidence:
The 2026 Agent Skills ecosystem report citing SkillsBench analyzed 47,150 public skills, found an average quality score of 6.2/12, and reported that curated skills improved agent pass rates by +16.2 percentage points (https://agentman.ai/blog/agent-skills-ecosystem-report-2026).
A September 2026 structured review of 26 agent skills against Anthropic skill-authoring guidance and the agentskills.io specification produced 152 concrete findings (https://github.com/fabiandistler/agents/issues/325; specification: https://agentskills.io/home).

Honest boundary: these signals establish that skill quality varies measurably and that evaluation demand exists; they are not popularity or adoption data. Passing this skill's checks is not proof of safety or runtime effectiveness.

title: Time-travel Debugging
description: Rewind an agent run to a prior checkpoint, inspect or modify state, and re-execute from that point while preserving checkpoint identity and separating diagnostic forks from production runs.
body:
Time-travel Debugging

Description
Time-travel debugging replays a stateful agent graph from a recorded checkpoint instead of repeating earlier work.
A checkpointer is required to inspect history. State edits create a diagnostic fork and should not silently mutate the original production run.
The exact checkpoint API depends on the graph runtime; the example below uses the LangGraph interface already described by this skill.

Inputs / Outputs

Reference Workflow

Diagnostic Protocol
Capture the production  and checkpoint identifier.
Verify that the checkpoint exists before replaying.
Replay the unmodified checkpoint first to establish a baseline.
Create a separate diagnostic thread before mutating state.
Record the state patch and reason for the fork.
Compare the forked result with the baseline.
Never overwrite production state merely to make a test pass.

Failure Modes

Reproducibility Limits
Checkpoint replay restores graph state, not the external world.
HTTP responses, clocks, random seeds, model outputs, databases, and tool side effects can differ unless captured or stubbed.
A replay should therefore report which external inputs were restored and which were live.

Validation Rules
The target checkpoint must exist before replay.
Diagnostic state changes must use a distinct run identity.
State patches must conform to the graph's state contract.
Replay results must not be presented as identical to production unless external effects were controlled.
Checkpoint identifiers and state changes should be recorded for auditability.

Security Boundaries
Checkpoint state can contain prompts, tool arguments, secrets, or user data.
Do not expose checkpoint contents to unauthorized users, logs, or model prompts merely for debugging convenience.
State patches must not be allowed to bypass authorization or approval gates.

Provenance
The workflow is runtime-specific at the API boundary and intentionally does not pin a LangGraph release here.
The conceptual guarantees are checkpoint lookup, controlled state replay, and diagnostic isolation; verify exact runtime APIs against the deployed version.

title: Tool Invention
description: Close capability gaps by designing, implementing, and validating new tools at runtime when no existing tool fits, with each invented tool reviewed, tested, and registered before reuse.
body:
Tool Invention

Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

An agent that only uses the tools it was given stalls the first time a task needs a missing primitive. Tool invention closes that gap deliberately: confirm the gap is real, write a minimal contract, implement with tests, validate on held-out cases, and register the tool for reuse. The discipline is what separates invention from improvisation — an invented tool is a durable artifact, not a one-off hack.

When to Use

Use when a repeated workaround shows a missing primitive: the same task fails or degrades across sessions and no registered tool covers it.

Do not invent tools to bypass an existing restriction; a guardrail that blocks a capability is a boundary, not a gap.

Inputs

Procedure
Confirm the gap: search the tool registry and prove no existing tool fits, citing the failure evidence.
Write a minimal contract: purpose, typed inputs and outputs, failure modes, and authority requirements.
Implement the smallest tool that satisfies the contract; nothing speculative.
Test against representative cases plus held-out cases the contract implies but the task did not show.
Review the tool (critic pass or second review) for correctness and boundary violations before first use.
Register the tool with a version and changelog; retire it when usage ends.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Invented tools inherit no authority. They must pass the same permission checks as pre-registered tools, must not wrap prohibited capabilities, and must be registered with their authority requirements declared. Invention of a tool that circumvents any security boundary is prohibited, not discouraged.

title: App Readiness Probing
description: Probe a launched application with an ordered, bounded check sequence and an injectable clock so downstream computer-use actions begin only once the app verifiably accepts them.
body:
App Readiness Probing

Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

An app process being alive does not mean its UI is usable: windows take time, ports open late, and services initialize in order. Readiness probing turns “it started” into evidence — an ordered list of checks re-evaluated on a fixed schedule until every check holds within a declared budget. The probe fails loudly when the budget is spent, carrying the elapsed time and the checks that still failed.

When to Use

Use after launching or connecting to an application — local desktop app, remote VM, or headed service — before any scripted interaction with its UI.

Do not use for continuous health monitoring of long-lived services; that is infrastructure probing, which has different lifecycle rules.

Inputs

Procedure
Define each check against an externally observable condition — listening port, window present, login prompt visible — never against process liveness alone.
Order checks by dependency: earlier checks must hold before later ones can be meaningful.
Evaluate every check each cycle in a fixed order, computing readiness as all-checks-hold.
Return the elapsed time at first success so startup cost is measured, not guessed.
On budget expiry, fail with elapsed time plus the list of still-failing checks.
Bind the budget to an injectable clock so probes replay identically in tests.
Re-measure the budget after environment changes; a budget tuned once is a stale budget.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Probing grants no authority; it only observes. Probes must use the same authenticated session the actions will use and must not probe systems outside the automation’s declared scope.

title: Desktop Notification Triage
description: Classify desktop notifications into act-now, batch, and ignore actions through explicit per-source rule tables with deduplication so an agent’s attention is allocated by policy, not reflex.
body:
Desktop Notification Triage

Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A notification stream is an attention budget under attack: calendars, builds, chats, and marketing all compete for the same reflex. Triage replaces reflex with a rule table — each source maps to a declared action class and deduplication key, repeated notifications collapse, and the output is an ordered action list. The rules are data, versioned with the corpus, and reviewable.

When to Use

Use when an agent or assistant monitors a desktop notification stream and must decide — by recorded policy — which notifications interrupt a task, which queue for later, and which are dropped.

Do not use for alerting humans from your own system; that direction has its own rate and severity contracts.

Inputs

Procedure
Give every source an explicit rule row before the stream starts; unmapped sources default to ignore, never to act.
Compute the deduplication key from the declared field; a missing key makes a notification non-deduplicatable and it is treated as unique.
Drop ignored and duplicate notifications before any action; duplicates never reach the action list.
Emit actions in arrival order as (source, action, key) triples so the decision trail is replayable.
Version the rule table with the agent configuration; triage behavior must be reproducible from the recorded rules.
Review dropped and duplicate counts periodically; a rule that drops everything real is a misconfiguration.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Notification contents can carry sensitive data and injected instructions. Triage classifies and filters but never executes content; instructions inside a notification are data, and acting on them requires the agent’s normal permission path.

title: Idle Detection
description: Detect user idle periods from timestamped activity events against an explicit threshold so background work can schedule itself into measured quiet windows.
body:
Idle Detection

Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

“The user looks away” is not an observation until it is defined: idle is a gap between timestamped activity events that meets a declared threshold. This skill computes idle periods from an activity log — each gap at or above the threshold is a quiet window, including the trailing gap up to now. The threshold is a policy number, recorded with the results, not an intuition.

When to Use

Use when background work — indexing, syncing, heavy computation — should run in measured quiet windows on a shared machine, or when session security needs an observable inactivity signal.

Do not use to infer user intent or presence for surveillance purposes; this contract measures gaps, not people.

Inputs

Procedure
Require sorted activity timestamps; unsorted input is rejected before gaps are computed.
Compute each gap between consecutive events; a gap at or above the threshold is an idle period.
Include the trailing gap from the last event to now when it meets the threshold.
Return periods as (start, end) pairs so downstream work can schedule against real windows.
Record the threshold alongside the results; a bare window list is uninterpretable later.
Re-validate the threshold after usage changes; the right quiet window is a moving target.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Activity timestamps are behavioral data about a person. Idle detection for scheduling must respect declared consent scopes, and its logs inherit the retention rules of the activity source.

title: Macro Recording
description: Record, normalize, and replay user-interface event sequences with deterministic compression of redundant input so repeated computer-use flows replay identically every time.
body:
Macro Recording

Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A recorded input sequence is only useful if it replays the same way twice. Raw event streams contain noise — intermediate mouse moves, doubled clicks, retraced paths — that makes replay fragile. This skill defines macro recording as a normalizing pipeline: capture typed events, compress redundant ones by explicit rules, store the script with its rules version, and replay from the normalized form only.

When to Use

Use when a repeated UI flow — setup, smoke checks, or form entry — should be captured once from real interaction and then replayed identically on demand.

Do not use to record credentials or one-time authorization flows; those inputs belong in secret stores, not in macro scripts.

Inputs

Procedure
Capture events as typed tuples — event type, target identifier, argument — in strict occurrence order.
Compress intermediate mouse-move events to the last position per continuous drag; never store every sampled point.
Merge rapid repeated clicks on one target into a double-click by the declared tolerance rule.
Keep the normalization rules versioned inside the macro; replay applies exactly the recorded version.
Replay strictly from the normalized script; raw captures are inputs, never the replay source.
Verify replay by a post-run state check, not by assuming the script worked.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

A macro is a recorded capability grant: it performs whatever its recording could perform. Keep macro scripts out of shared storage, exclude secrets at capture time, and scope replay to the environment it was recorded in.
