body:
Screen Recording

Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A screen recording turns transient UI behavior into reviewable evidence: a bug reproduces, a procedure demonstrates itself, a session leaves an audit trail. The mechanics are region selection, steady frame pacing, and reliable encoding; the judgment is what must never be in the frame and what happens to the file afterward.

When to Use

Use to reproduce a UI defect with full context, record a procedure for later replay, or produce task evidence of an automated desktop session.

Do not record covertly, and do not record sessions likely to contain credentials or personal input without an explicit policy permitting it.

Inputs

Procedure
Determine the capture scope; map logical coordinates to the physical monitor and DPI so the region is what you think it is.
Check consent and policy: close or exclude windows that may contain secrets or personal data before capture starts.
Configure deterministic pacing and a hard frame budget derived from duration and fps.
Capture; if the region moves (window drag), re-anchor or fail loudly rather than silently record the wrong area.
Encode with a standard codec, record a checksum, and write metadata (region, fps, duration, host).
Verify the result covers the intended interval before reporting success.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Screen recordings can contain credentials, personal data, and confidential documents. Record only what policy and consent permit, store with retention limits, restrict access, and treat the recording as sensitive until reviewed. Recordings of a user's screen without their knowledge are prohibited.

title: Screen Region Mapping
description: Map normalized screen coordinates onto integer pixel regions across logical resolutions and device pixel ratios so UI targets stay stable when displays or zoom levels change.
body:
Screen Region Mapping

Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Pixel coordinates are a fragile basis for automation: change the display scale or resolution and every stored target breaks. Normalized coordinates — 0..1 fractions of the logical screen — survive both. This skill defines the mapping contract in both directions: normalized to pixels for acting, pixels to normalized for recording, with the device pixel ratio explicit in every conversion so HiDPI displays compute correctly.

When to Use

Use when recorded UI targets must survive resolution, monitor, or zoom changes, or when screenshots from different device pixel ratios must be compared against one logical layout.

Do not use for text-based targets; element identifiers and accessibility trees are more stable than any coordinate scheme.

Inputs

Procedure
Store automation targets in normalized units; treat pixel coordinates as derived, disposable values.
Carry the device pixel ratio in every conversion; omitting it silently halves or doubles regions on HiDPI displays.
Convert each coordinate by multiplying normalized value, logical size, and dpr, rounding half away from zero.
Clamp pixel results to the physical screen bounds; off-screen regions are rejected, not wrapped.
Round-trip check critical regions: convert to pixels and back, and reject mappings that drift beyond a declared tolerance.
On multi-monitor setups, anchor normalized coordinates to the specific monitor’s logical size, never to the union of screens.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Screen regions describe where to act, not what may be acted on. Mapping grants no authority: every action derived from a region still passes the permission checks of the underlying automation.

Evidence

This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references:
MDN documentation for window.devicePixelRatio (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/devicePixelRatio).
Python’s round() documentation for rounding behavior (https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#round).

Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.

title: UI Element Waiting
description: Synchronize computer-use actions on observed UI state with bounded explicit-wait loops, injected clocks, and timeout budgets instead of fixed sleeps so automation is deterministic and fails fast.
body:
UI Element Waiting

Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A fixed sleep is a guess that wastes time when the app is fast and fails when it is slow. An explicit wait replaces the guess with a contract: poll a state predicate on a fixed interval until it holds or a declared budget expires. With an injected clock the loop is testable offline, and the wait either returns the observed ready time or fails with evidence of how much budget was spent.

When to Use

Use whenever an automation must act on an element that appears asynchronously — after launch, navigation, or a slow update — and the failure mode of a timeout should be an explicit error rather than a mistimed click.

Do not use to mask an application bug; if a reasonable budget never suffices, fix the application or shorten the flow instead of raising timeouts.

Inputs

Procedure
Define the readiness predicate on observable state — DOM presence, pixel match, or API flag — never on elapsed time alone.
Declare timeout and poll interval before starting the wait; defaults must come from policy, not from the call site’s mood.
Compute the deadline from the injected clock so tests run deterministically offline.
Evaluate the predicate at least once before advancing time, so already-ready elements return immediately.
On timeout, fail with the budget spent and the last observed state; a silent None return hides the evidence.
Record observed wait times per element so budgets are tuned on measurements, not folklore.
Never nest waits to synthesize longer budgets; raise the declared budget instead.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Waiting on UI state grants no authority over the application. An automation observing readiness may act only within its permitted action set; polling must respect the target app’s load and authentication boundaries.

body:
Browser Profile Management

Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A browser profile is a bag of authenticated identity and accumulated state. The skill covers defining a profile blueprint, creating isolated contexts from it rather than mutating a shared session, restoring saved storage state when persistence is required, exporting state after authenticated runs, and proving teardown left the base profile untouched. Isolation is the default because concurrent writes to one profile corrupt state and make runs order-dependent.

When to Use

Use when automation needs persistent login state, parallel isolated sessions, or reproducible browser environments with consistent locale, timezone, and viewport settings.

Do not share a single logged-in profile across parallel runs. Concurrent sessions on one profile corrupt storage state and produce flaky, order-dependent results.

Inputs

Procedure
Define the profile blueprint: base settings, storage state source, and the required isolation level.
Create a fresh context from the blueprint rather than mutating a shared browser session.
Restore saved storage state where persistence is required and record exactly what was restored.
Apply consistent locale, timezone, viewport, and permission settings for reproducibility.
Export storage state at the end of authenticated runs for reuse, without logging any secrets.
Tear down the context and confirm no state leaked into the base profile.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

A profile is a credential by another name. Treat exported storage state as a secret: restrict file permissions, scope each profile to the narrowest account the task needs, and never share profiles across operators or environments.

File Download Verification

Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A download is not finished when the file appears; it is finished when it is verified. The skill arms download handling before triggering the event, waits for completion with a bounded timeout, then checks size, media type, and checksum against expectations before the artifact is allowed downstream. Failures quarantine the file rather than silently passing it along.

When to Use

Use when automation must fetch files through an authenticated or interactive browser session and must prove the result is the expected artifact rather than a truncated or substituted payload.

Do not trust the downloaded filename or extension. Verify content by checksum and media type before any downstream use, because names and extensions are attacker-controllable.

Inputs

Procedure
Arm download handling before triggering the event so the stream is captured from the start.
Trigger the download and capture the suggested filename and the serving URL as provenance.
Wait for completion with a bounded timeout; a partial file must fail, not pass.
Verify size, media type, and when provided checksum against the expectations.
Store the artifact under a collision-free normalized name with its provenance metadata.
Report verification results and quarantine any file that fails a check.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Downloads cross a trust boundary into local storage. Verify the serving origin, quarantine unexpected artifacts, and never execute or open a downloaded file before verification, because the browser session may have been steered to serve attacker-controlled content.

Iframe Handling

Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Iframe handling turns a flat page into a tree of documents. The skill covers enumerating frames, resolving the target frame by identity rather than by selector alone, re-scoping lookups to the frame document, and proving the current scope before and after every action. The core discipline is that a selector never identifies an element on its own in a framed page; a (frame, selector) pair does.

When to Use

Use when a target page embeds content in one or more iframes: embedded forms, payment widgets, media players, sandboxed previews, or third-party embeds that must be automated or audited.

Do not assume a single flat DOM. The same selector can resolve in several frames, and acting inside the wrong frame produces plausible-looking but incorrect results.

Inputs

Procedure
Enumerate all frames in the page with their name, URL, and nesting depth before any interaction.
Resolve the target frame by selector, name, or URL pattern; prefer URL identity when selectors collide.
Enter the frame and re-scope all subsequent lookups to its document root.
Assert a frame-specific element exists before acting; a missing anchor means the scope is wrong.
Perform the action inside the frame, treating every lookup as frame-relative, never global.
Exit to the top document explicitly and re-assert scope before continuing with other tasks.

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Iframes frequently embed third-party content, and entering a frame moves input across an origin boundary. Verify the frame origin before typing anything into it, never inject credentials into unverified origins, and record which origins received input as part of the audit trail.

title: Infinite Scroll Handling
description: Extract complete data sets from pages that reveal content incrementally on scroll, with termination detection, batch deduplication, and bounded run budgets.
body:
Infinite Scroll Handling

Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Infinite scroll pages never announce that they are finished. The skill treats scrolling as a batch protocol: extract the visible viewport, scroll one viewport height, wait for the page to settle, deduplicate against what is already collected, and terminate on a budget, a sentinel element, or a run of empty batches. Each batch is persisted as it arrives so a late failure loses only the tail.

When to Use

Use when a feed, gallery, or results list reveals content as the user scrolls and the full set must be collected rather than sampled.

Do not scroll until the page stops by itself without a hard budget. Some feeds generate content forever and will exhaust memory, time, or rate limits before they exhaust content.

Inputs

Procedure
Extract the initial viewport before any scroll and record it as the first batch.
Scroll by one viewport height and wait for the network or DOM to settle before extracting.
Re-extract and deduplicate against already-collected batches using stable item keys.
Terminate when the budget is hit, the sentinel appears, or several consecutive batches yield nothing new.
Persist each batch before scrolling again so a late failure loses only the tail.
Report the collected count, batch count, and the exact termination reason.

Outputs

Runnable Example

body:
Pagination Following

Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Paginated content hides most of the corpus behind a “next” affordance, and a naive loop either stops early or spins forever on a circular link. This skill defines pagination traversal as a bounded graph walk: each page declares how its next link is identified, a visited set rejects cycles, and a page cap bounds the walk even when the listing is generated adversarially.

When to Use

Use when scraping or crawling structured listings — search results, catalogs, archives — that expose next-page links or numbered pages.

Do not use for infinite-scroll feeds that expose no pagination affordance; those need event-driven capture, not link following.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare the next-link selector convention up front — rel=next, a labeled link, or a numbered URL scheme — and use it consistently.
Normalize each next URL before comparison so parameter noise cannot disguise a cycle.
Record every visited page in the visited set; a next URL already present is a loop, and traversal stops with the loop identified.
Stop at the first missing next link; absence is the listing’s terminal, not an error.
Enforce the page cap even when the listing keeps offering links; unbounded traversal is a policy violation.
Emit the visited sequence plus a terminal reason — terminal, loop, or cap — so the walk is auditable.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Pagination traversal is still fetching; robots rules, rate limits, and terms of service apply to every page visited. The page cap is a politeness bound as much as a correctness one.

body:
Robots.txt Parsing

Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Politeness on the web starts with a parsed contract, not string matching. robots.txt groups directives by user-agent, allows and disallows paths, requests a crawl delay, and points to sitemaps. This skill defines a minimal deterministic parser — grouping, per-agent rule lists, sitemap collection — and a query interface so “may this agent fetch this path” is a testable function of recorded rules.

When to Use

Use before any crawl or scrape touches a new host, and as the standing policy engine that answers per-path fetch questions during crawling.

Do not use robots.txt parsing as a legal position; it encodes machine etiquette, and separate permission, terms, and law still apply.

Inputs

Procedure
Strip comments and blank lines before directive parsing; directives survive, decoration does not.
Group rules by user-agent block: directives following a User-agent line belong to that agent until the next one.
Collect Sitemap lines globally; they are host-level, not per-agent.
Store Allow, Disallow, and Crawl-delay as ordered per-agent rule lists.
Answer path queries by longest-prefix match, with Allow and Disallow resolved by rule specificity.
Treat parse failure or absence of robots.txt under the declared fallback policy — ask-permissive or ask-conservative — chosen once and recorded.
Re-fetch robots.txt at a bounded interval during long crawls; a cached policy outlives its welcome.

Shadow DOM Interaction

Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Shadow DOM hides component internals behind a boundary that ordinary selectors cannot cross. The skill covers probing for shadow roots, composing locator chains across each boundary, asserting that a composed chain resolves to exactly one element, and respecting closed roots by interacting only through the interfaces a component exposes. Every boundary crossed is recorded so a failure can be traced to the correct layer.

When to Use

Use when component libraries or web components encapsulate markup in shadow roots and standard selectors cannot reach the interactive elements inside them.

Do not force open closed shadow roots through internal framework APIs. A closed root is a component contract; interact through its exposed methods and attributes only.

Inputs

Procedure
Probe candidate hosts to determine which ones carry shadow roots and whether each root is open or closed.
Choose piercing mode when the automation engine supports it; otherwise walk each shadow boundary explicitly.
Compose a locator chain across the boundaries and record the full path from the page root to the target.
Assert the composed chain resolves to exactly one element; zero or many results both mean the chain is wrong.
Interact through exposed methods or attributes when the root is closed instead of bypassing the boundary.
Record every boundary crossed so failures can be attributed to the correct layer of the component tree.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Shadow DOM is an encapsulation boundary that some components rely on for security assumptions. Bypassing it can expose internal state that the component author intended to hide; probe only what the task requires and never exfiltrate internals beyond the run.

title: URL Normalization
description: Normalize URLs by lowercasing scheme and host, removing default ports and fragments, sorting query parameters, and collapsing path noise so identical resources compare equal.
body:
URL Normalization

Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Two strings that differ can still name the same page: mixed case, an explicit :443, a stray fragment, unsorted parameters. Naive deduplication misses them all. Normalization applies a declared, ordered set of transformations — scheme and host lowercased, default ports removed, empty fragments dropped, parameters sorted — producing one canonical form per resource so equality checks mean something.

When to Use

Use before storing, deduplicating, or comparing URLs from crawls, logs, or user input, and as the canonicalization step of any fetch cache key.

Do not normalize URLs whose case-sensitive path is part of an API contract; preserve those verbatim and exclude them from normalization by policy.

Inputs

Procedure
Split the URL into scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment before any transformation.
Lowercase scheme and host; they are case-insensitive by URL grammar.
Drop ports that are the scheme default (443 for https, 80 for http); keep non-default ports.
Collapse an empty fragment; when stripping is on, drop any fragment per policy.
Sort query parameters by name then value so parameter order stops producing duplicates.
Normalize the path — collapse duplicate slashes, resolve dot segments — without changing case.
Return the canonical string and use it, not the input, as every comparison and cache key.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Normalization rewrites identifiers; it must never rewrite authority. Credentials embedded in URLs are a separate defect to flag and strip deliberately, not silently, and canonical forms inherit the trust level of their source.

URL Rate Limiting

Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Every fetcher needs a throttle it can explain: a rate, a burst, and a per-host scope, enforced by a token bucket rather than by sleeps between calls. This skill defines that bucket — capacity and refill rate per host, an injectable clock for deterministic tests, and an allow/deny answer per request — so a crawl’s politeness is a recorded contract that can be measured, tuned, and logged.

When to Use

Use whenever an agent fetches from hosts it does not own, when a host declares a crawl delay, or before any parallel fetch loop could otherwise stampede a single origin.

Do not use to throttle your own outbound API quota when the platform enforces it already; double throttling wastes time without adding politeness.

Inputs

Procedure
Create one bucket per host; a shared bucket lets one fast host starve every other.
Refill tokens by elapsed time multiplied by the declared rate, capped at the burst capacity.
Admit a request only when a full token is available; deny without consuming.
Honour host-declared crawl delays by treating them as a lower bound on the rate.
Log allow and deny decisions with timestamps so backpressure is measured, not inferred.
Never bypass the bucket on error paths; retries consume tokens like any other request.
Inject the clock in tests so refill arithmetic replays deterministically.

Rate limiting is a politeness boundary, not an authorization one. Passing the bucket grants no right to fetch; robots rules, terms of service, and authentication still apply, and denial must degrade gracefully rather than escalate.

URL Redirect Tracing

Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A URL that redirects is a claim about where content really lives, and the chain matters: shorteners launder destinations, loops waste budgets, and mixed http-to-https hops change the security posture mid-chain. This skill records every hop as (from, to, status-class), detects cycles, and refuses to follow past a declared hop cap.

When to Use

Use when resolving shortened or syndicated links into their final targets, when auditing where a stored URL actually lands, or before treating a fetched origin as trustworthy.

Do not use to bypass a site’s redirect intent; if a host routes you to a consent or login page, that response is the answer, not an obstacle.

Inputs

Procedure
Record each hop as it happens — from URL, to URL, status class — never reconstruct the chain from memory after the fact.
Normalize URLs before cycle comparison; a loop hidden by a trailing slash is still a loop.
Treat a repeated URL as a cycle and stop immediately, reporting the loop entry point.
Stop at the hop cap and report it distinctly from a terminal resolution.
Preserve the full chain in the result; a bare final URL without its chain is unauditable.
Flag scheme downgrades (https to http) in the chain as a security-relevant event.

body:
Web Archive Lookup

Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Pages change and disappear, and an agent that cited one yesterday may need the bytes it saw, not today’s revision. Web archives answer with timestamped snapshots, but only if requests are built correctly: a canonical URL form, a timestamp in the archive’s format, and an explicit rule for choosing among nearby snapshots. This skill defines that lookup as a deterministic computation.

When to Use

Use when verifying a citation against a prior page state, recovering deleted content for evidence, or comparing a page across time.

Do not use archived copies as a substitute for fetching the live page when current information is the requirement; archives lag and the present is authoritative.

Inputs

Procedure
Normalize the URL before requesting archives; equivalent spellings fragment the snapshot history.
Construct the archive request with the normalized URL and the requested timestamp in the documented format.
When the exact timestamp is absent, select the nearest earlier snapshot under a declared rule and record both requested and selected times.
Report when no snapshot precedes the request; an empty history is an answer, not an error to retry.
Record the archive’s identifier for the chosen snapshot so the same evidence can be retrieved again.
Treat archived content as historical evidence with its capture date attached; undated citation of an archive is a defect.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Archived pages are third-party records, not the original source’s word; they can be incomplete or manipulated upstream. Archive lookups grant no authority over the original site and inherit the archive’s own terms of use.

title: Data Anonymization
description: Transform data sets to reduce re-identification risk using suppression, generalization, and pseudonymization, with k-anonymity checks and honest reporting of residual risk.
body:
Data Anonymization

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Anonymization is measured, not declared. The skill covers classifying fields into direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers, and sensitive attributes, applying the policy of transforms, then measuring what remains: equivalence-class sizes over quasi-identifier combinations, records below threshold, and utility lost to generalization. Output that cannot meet the threshold is suppressed or further generalized rather than passed through with a false label.

When to Use

Use when data containing personal or identifying elements must be shared, published, or analyzed outside its origin context.

Do not treat column deletion as anonymization. Remaining quasi-identifiers such as postcode, timestamps, and rare value combinations re-identify most individuals when combined.

Inputs

Procedure
Classify every field as direct identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive, or neutral before transforming.
Apply the policy: suppress or tokenize direct identifiers and generalize quasi-identifiers.
Measure residual risk, including k-anonymity over every quasi-identifier combination.
Report the equivalence-class distribution and the records that fall below the threshold.
Suppress or further generalize below-threshold records instead of passing them through.
Document the transforms applied so the output can never be presented as raw source data.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Anonymization failures cause irreversible privacy harm. Never claim the output is anonymous without measuring residual risk, keep re-identification mappings under separate access control, and stop and escalate when the threshold cannot be met instead of shipping weakly protected data.

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Data Lineage

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A number without ancestry is a rumor with formatting. This skill records ancestry as a first-class artifact: every dataset declares its inputs, the transformation and code version that produced it, and the outputs that depend on it. Lineage answers two questions the moment they are asked — where did this come from, and what breaks if this changes — and a lineage graph that cannot answer both is decoration, not documentation.

When to Use

Use for datasets that feed decisions, reports, or models — anywhere a wrong number needs to be traced to its source or an upstream change needs its blast radius known.

Do not hand-maintain lineage for throwaway exploratory scratch data; capture it where outputs persist and matter, and let the pipeline write the graph.

Inputs

Procedure
Record inputs precisely: which upstream datasets, at which versions or snapshots, fed the transformation.
Record the transformation itself — code version, parameters, and environment — enough to reproduce the output.
Write lineage at run time from the pipeline itself, not by hand afterward; hand-maintained lineage is yesterday's graph.
Register outputs symmetrically: a dataset knows what it fed, so impact analysis can walk forward as easily as backward.
Attach the lineage record to the data — a table property, a manifest, a catalog entry — not to a wiki page.
On any upstream change, consult the forward graph before it merges: blast radius is a lineage query, not a guess.

Data Profiling

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Every analysis rests on beliefs about its data: that ids are unique, that the date column is a date, that the two category columns relate the way they did last quarter. Profiling replaces those beliefs with measurements: counts, distinct values, null rates, ranges, and distribution shapes, recorded per column and compared over time. The profile is not the analysis — it is the ground the analysis stands on, and a profile that changed since last week is often the whole explanation for a number that stopped making sense.

When to Use

Use when a dataset is new to you, before publication or reporting on it, and periodically on datasets assumed stable.

Do not profile a known-stable, schema-verified table on every read; repeated profiling of unchanged data is cost without information.

Inputs

Procedure
Profile structure first: column names, types, row count, and how those differ from any recorded schema.
Measure completeness per column — null rates and default values — and distinctness: cardinality and top values.
Profile ranges and distributions for numeric and temporal columns, recording min, max, and shape, not just the mean.
Diff against the baseline profile and flag every metric that moved beyond its historical band.
Record the profile with the dataset version and date, so future comparisons have something concrete to diff.
Turn anomalies into constraints: a property that surprised you is a rule for the validation boundary.

Security and Authority Boundary

Profiles are exfiltration-shaped: cardinalities, top values, and ranges of sensitive columns can disclose individual records, so profiling outputs on restricted data inherit its access scope and profiling jobs must not write measurements to stores more public than the data itself could reach.

body:
Data Validation

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Data arrives wrong more often than it arrives late: nulls where keys live, strings where numbers were promised, duplicate rows quietly doubling a metric. This skill moves checking to the boundary: constraints are declared alongside the pipeline, every batch is validated on arrival, and a violation stops the data instead of following it downstream. The essential move is declaring expectations explicitly — an undeclared constraint cannot be checked, and an unchecked constraint eventually becomes a wrong number someone acted on.

When to Use

Use at every ingestion boundary — files, API feeds, database extracts — and before anything feeds reporting, training, or user-visible output.

Do not validate beyond what consumers depend on; a constraint nobody relies on still costs every batch and fails runs for no operational reason.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare the schema first — column names, types, nullability — and version it beside the pipeline that enforces it.
Add value constraints that consumers actually rely on: ranges, enum membership, uniqueness of keys, referential joins.
Run validation on arrival, per batch, and collect all violations rather than stopping at the first.
Route failures by severity: hard violations quarantine the batch, soft ones are logged with counts and rates.
Report violation statistics as data — failure rates by rule over time — so drift is visible before it becomes an outage.
Change the schema deliberately: a constraint change ships as a reviewed edit with a migration, not as a hotfix to silence a failing rule.

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Validation reports quote offending values: constraint failures on sensitive columns must surface the shape of the violation without reproducing the raw value in logs, and validation stages should inherit the access scope of the data they check.

!Dependency Status

Embedding Generation

Description

Embedding generation converts arbitrary inputs (most commonly text) into fixed-dimensional dense vectors that encode semantic similarity: similar inputs land near each other in vector space. The vectors are produced by a frozen pre-trained model and consumed by retrieval, clustering, classification, and recommendation systems.

This skill covers the production-grade contract: deterministic batching to maximise throughput, content-hash caching so you don't re-embed unchanged inputs, dimension reduction (via Matryoshka truncation when supported), and the silent-failure modes — wrong tokenizer, mixing dimensions, missing normalisation — that bite teams six months in.

When to Use
You need a vector representation that downstream code (vector store, classifier, ranker) can consume.
The input is text (most common), or images/audio with a multimodal embedding model.
You're embedding once and querying many times → cache by content hash; embeddings are deterministic for fixed model+content.
Don't use when a sparse keyword index (BM25, tf-idf) is sufficient or when you need a probability distribution rather than a similarity vector.

description: Process new data as it arrives instead of reprocessing the whole corpus — checkpoints, watermarks, and late-arrival handling — so cost stays flat as history grows.
body:
Incremental Processing

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A pipeline that recomputes everything on every run is a pipeline with a half-life: the corpus grows, the run lengthens, and the day arrives where the run no longer fits between the arrivals. This skill switches the unit of work from the dataset to the delta: the process tracks what it has already consumed, takes only the new records past that mark, and handles the stragglers — late, out-of-order, or corrected records — by explicit rule rather than by accident.

When to Use

Use when data arrives continuously or the corpus is large enough that full recomputation no longer fits its window — event streams, append-only logs, growing tables.

Do not add incremental machinery to small, fully recomputable datasets; a full pass over a small table is simpler, idempotent by construction, and easier to reason about.

Inputs

Procedure
Pick the position marker — an offset, a timestamp, or a sequence column — that strictly advances as new data arrives.
Persist a checkpoint after each processed unit, and make downstream updates idempotent so a replay from the checkpoint is safe.
Process only records past the checkpoint, committing the new checkpoint only after the unit is durably processed.
Handle late arrivals by rule: bounded wait behind a watermark, correction events, or explicit drop — never by silent overwrite.
Measure lag — arrival time to processed time — and alarm when the checkpoint stops advancing, because a stalled marker is the failure mode.
Periodically reconcile the incremental result against a full recomputation, so drift between the two is caught at a known cost.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Incremental state is attack surface: checkpoints record positions and the process holds partial aggregates, so both must inherit the access scope of the source data, and late-arrival or correction paths — which can rewrite aggregates — deserve the same authorization checks as the primary path.

body:
Missing Data Imputation

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

How values are missing carries as much signal as the values themselves, and a single global fill rule such as zero-for-everything destroys that signal. This skill defines the disciplined loop: profile per-column missingness, pick a strategy per column, fit fill values on training rows only, and record an imputation mask so every filled cell stays identifiable for later audit.

When to Use

Use when training or reporting data has missing cells and the fill rule affects the result.

Do not use for already-masked experimental data where missingness is part of the design; that case is analysis configuration, not imputation.

Inputs

Procedure
Profile every column: missing count, missing rate, and the pattern of co-missingness across rows.
Classify each column’s missingness mechanism before choosing a strategy; uniform filling across mechanisms is a smell.
Choose a strategy per column and record why it was chosen.
Fit fill values on the declared fit scope only; never let test or future rows influence a fill value.
Apply fills to a copy; the original rows stay untouched for audit.
Record an imputation mask alongside the filled data so every filled cell is identifiable later.
Re-profile after filling and compare distributions; a fill that moves a distribution needs a second look.
Document the mask’s retention period; the mask is analytical metadata, not a permanent record.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Imputing values grants no authority to invent records. Filled cells are estimates and must remain identifiable as such through the mask. Data subject to privacy or retention limits keeps those limits through the whole loop: profiling, filling, and the mask inherit them.

title: Stream Processing
description: Process unbounded event streams with windowed aggregation, watermarking, and exactly-once handling, keeping results correct under late arrival, replay, and backpressure.
body:
Stream Processing

Category: Data | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Stream processing computes over data that never stops arriving. The skill covers partitioning by key, defining windows with explicit late-arrival policy, advancing watermarks to bound results, emitting windowed aggregates, and handling replay and failure through idempotent sinks. Correctness comes from declared semantics: at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes, or exactly-once where the engine supports transactional state.

When to Use

Use when events must be aggregated, joined, or alerted on as they arrive rather than in batch: telemetry, click streams, sensor feeds, or transaction flows.

Do not treat an unbounded stream as if it were a growing table. Without windows and watermarks, results never finalize and memory grows without bound.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare delivery semantics first: at-least-once with idempotent sinks, or exactly-once with transactional state.
Partition by key so per-key ordering holds; record the partitioner choice.
Define windows with an explicit type, size, and allowed lateness; never use defaults silently.
Advance watermarks from event time and emit window results when the watermark closes the window.
Handle late events per policy: update the result if the sink allows, or route them to a side output.
On failure, restore state from the checkpoint and replay from the committed offset, proving no double emission.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Streams often carry personal or operational data at high velocity. Scope access at the topic or partition level, avoid enriching events with unrelated lookups mid-stream, and make sinks tamper-evident because stream outputs frequently drive automated decisions.

Synthetic Data Generation

Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Synthetic data replaces sensitive or scarce data with records generated from a model or a specification. The skill covers choosing a generation strategy: fully synthetic from declared distributions, or fitted to a source with constraints that prevent memorization, then validating the output for statistical fidelity, referential integrity, and leakage of real records. The output is labeled synthetic, with its provenance recorded so it can never be mistaken for production data.

When to Use

Use when development, testing, or demonstrations need realistic data volumes and shapes without access to real personal or proprietary records.

Do not present synthetic data as a privacy solution by default. Naive fitting can memorize rare records; privacy claims require measurement, not generation method labels.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare the schema and per-field distributions, or fit distributions to a source sample.
State the fidelity target: which statistics and correlations the output must preserve.
Generate records with a fixed seed for reproducibility, applying constraints during generation.
Validate the output for schema conformance, statistical fidelity, and referential integrity.
Check for leakage: nearest-neighbor overlap with any real source records must be explained.
Label the data set synthetic with provenance, seed, and generator version.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Synthetic data lowers exposure but is not automatically safe: a poorly fitted generator can reproduce real individuals. Measure overlap against source data, never mix synthetic and production stores, and label outputs so downstream consumers cannot mistake them for real records.

Brand Voice Development

Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A brand voice is a small set of decisions applied consistently, not a mood board. The skill covers extracting voice traits from brand values, defining each trait as a position on a tone axis with do-and-never examples, writing vocabulary and punctuation rules, and validating drafts by rewriting the same sample in the defined voice. A voice is done when an unfamiliar writer can apply the spec and pass a blind consistency check.

When to Use

Use when an organization needs its writing to sound consistent across channels, writers, and formats, from support replies to marketing copy.

Do not describe the voice only with adjectives such as friendly and bold. Without axis positions, vocabulary rules, and contrast examples, every writer interpolates differently.

Inputs

Procedure
Extract candidate voice traits from brand values and the audience relationship.
Reduce the traits to three to five axes and pick a position on each, with rationale.
Write do-and-never examples per trait so contrast is explicit, not implied.
Define vocabulary rules: preferred terms, banned terms, and grammar choices.
Rewrite one canonical sample passage in the new voice and annotate every change.
Run a blind consistency check with an unfamiliar writer before publishing the spec.

Character Design

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A character is a contract with the reader: the way they speak, what they want, what they cannot do. Breaking that contract by convenience is how stories lose trust. This skill defines a character as a structured profile — identity, motivation, capabilities with explicit limits, and voice rules — plus a beat sheet for their arc, so consistency is checkable against a record instead of remembered vibes.

When to Use

Use when introducing a recurring character into any narrative work — prose, games, scripts — whose behavior must stay consistent across scenes and writers.

Do not use for background figures who appear once; a full profile for a walk-on role is overhead.

Inputs

Procedure
Write the profile before the character acts: motivation, capability set with explicit limits, and voice rules with examples.
State what the character cannot do; limits are what make capability meaningful.
Plan the arc as an ordered beat list and check it contains the required beat types before writing.
Check every written scene against the profile; out-of-character action requires either a new beat that earns it or a profile revision.
Keep the profile versioned with the work so any scene can be traced to the character state it assumed.
Give each distinct character a distinguishable voice rule set; interchangeable voices are a design failure.

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Color Palette Generation

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A palette is a system of roles with constraints, not a set of attractive colors. The skill covers deriving palettes from a base hue using declared harmony strategies, assigning roles such as background, surface, text, accent, and state, then verifying the assignments against WCAG contrast thresholds and the expected display contexts. A palette ships only with its measured contrast table, because the ratios are the part that makes it usable.

When to Use

Use when an interface, brand, or document needs a coherent set of colors with known contrast behavior across text, states, and backgrounds.

Do not judge a palette by its swatches alone. Colors that look harmonious side by side can fail legibility the moment one becomes text on another.

Inputs

Procedure
Convert the base color to a working space such as HSL or OKLCH and derive candidate steps.
Generate harmony candidates per the chosen strategy, keeping lightness and saturation controlled.
Assign roles: background, surface, text, accent, and state colors.
Compute contrast ratios for every text-on-background pairing the design needs.
Adjust lightness until all required pairings pass WCAG AA, or better where the brief demands.
Emit the palette with hex values, roles, and the measured contrast table.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Palettes carry accessibility obligations in many products. Do not soften measured thresholds to save an aesthetic, and test with color-vision deficiency simulation before shipping state colors that users must distinguish to operate safely.

description: Write character dialogue with explicit speaker turns, subtext layers, and mechanical exchange checks so conversations stay consistent, purposeful, and attributable line by line.
body:
Dialogue Writing

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Dialogue has mechanics and meaning: every line belongs to a speaker, turns should not blur into monologue by accident, and what a character says should rarely be exactly what they mean. This skill treats dialogue as structured data — (speaker, text) turns with optional subtext — plus checks for alternation, tagging, and emptiness, so the craft decisions sit on a verifiable exchange structure.

When to Use

Use when writing scenes of two or more voices where speaker attribution and turn structure must stay clean — prose, scripts, or interactive fiction.

Do not use for interior monologue; unattributed thought is not dialogue and follows different rules.

Inputs

Procedure
Write every line as an explicit (speaker, text) turn; unattributed lines are a structural defect, not a style.
Run the exchange checks before polishing prose: same-speaker runs must be intentional, empty lines removed.
Give each line a purpose — information, pressure, or relationship change — and cut lines with none.
Set the subtext deliberately; when text equals meaning, that sameness should be the decision, not the default.
Read voices against their speaker rules; a line that fits no voice is a draft error.
Keep the exchange table with the draft so revisions do not silently drop speakers or turns.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Dialogue written in real people’s voices — impressions of living individuals — carries defamation and dignity risks. Fictional voices should stay fictional, and borrowed real-world dialect deserves researched respect.

description: Design and tune game mechanics as rule systems with resources, loops, and failure states, documenting economy balance and player choice structure before implementation.
body:
Game Mechanic Design

Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A mechanic is a rule system, not a feature name. The skill covers expressing mechanics as resources, actions, and loops; defining the core loop and its failure and mastery states; tuning numbers against an economy model so strategies stay diverse; and documenting the system precisely enough to prototype and critique before any art exists. Designs are tested on paper against degenerate strategies first.

When to Use

Use when a new game, mode, or system needs its rules designed and balanced before implementation, or when an existing mechanic needs retuning.

Do not balance with intuition alone. Without an economy model, dominant strategies and dead mechanics ship and are expensive to fix after players learn them.

Inputs

Procedure
Express the mechanic as resources, actions, and a loop that connects them.
Define the failure states and the mastery curve, including how each failure teaches.
Model the economy: sources, sinks, and exchange rates between resources.
Simulate representative strategies on paper and identify dominant or dead options.
Tune numbers until distinct strategies stay viable within the target session length.
Document the system with the loop diagram, the economy table, and open risks.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Mechanic designs include monetization structures that can be manipulative. Model the economy honestly, disclose odds where randomized purchases exist, and avoid dark patterns that exploit loss aversion or sunk cost in players.

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Naming by staring at a blank page produces the first defensible option; naming by generation produces the space of options and then chooses. This skill defines name generation as a constrained search: a morpheme inventory, a construction pattern, a banned list, and collision checks against existing names — producing a reproducible candidate set instead of a lucky guess.

When to Use

Use when a product, character, place, or brand needs a name and the process should explore the option space deliberately rather than seize the first idea.

Do not use where naming is externally fixed by standards, clients, or convention; constrained search cannot substitute for a mandated name.

Declare the inventories and construction rules before generating; free-form generation cannot be reproduced or audited.
Generate the full candidate set from the inventories under the construction rules.
Filter by the declared pattern so shape violations never reach review.
Apply the banned list and collision checks against existing names before presenting candidates.
Present candidates with their construction provenance — which morphemes and rules produced them.

Plot Structure

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Structure is the load-bearing frame a story hangs from: acts, beats, and their positions. Without declared positions, a “slow second act” is a feeling; with them, it is a measurable gap between the inciting event and the midpoint. This skill defines plot structure as a table — beats named, positioned on a 0–100 scale, and assigned to declared acts — so the shape is visible and every deviation is a decision.

When to Use

Use when planning or diagnosing a story’s shape — novels, screenplays, episodes — before or during drafting, or when a draft feels structurally off.

Do not use to impose structure on completed work by force; if a story resists the chosen form, change forms deliberately rather than mangle the story.

Inputs

Procedure
Choose the structural form first and declare its act boundaries on a normalized 0–100 scale.
Position each beat on the same scale; relative position is the contract, not chapter count.
Check that every beat falls inside exactly one act; boundary orphans indicate scale drift.
Check the form’s required beats are present and positioned within their expected ranges.
Report structural gaps — long stretches with no beat — as measurable intervals, not impressions.
Revise positions on evidence when pacing is off; the table is the plan of record.

Security and Authority Boundary

Poetry Forms

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A fixed form is a contract in counts: five and seven for the haiku, fourteen lines with a rhyme scheme for the sonnet. Meeting the contract by assertion is how “approximate haiku” happens. This skill treats form compliance as checkable arithmetic — per-line syllable counts against declared targets, line count against the form, rhyme pattern against the scheme — with the checks running before the poem is presented as done.

When to Use

Use when writing in a fixed form, when an exercise or publication requires exact form compliance, or when teaching forms where the mechanics matter.

Do not use for free verse; imposing fixed-form checks on open forms misreads the contract.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare the form’s numeric contract up front — syllable targets per line, line count, rhyme scheme.
Count syllables per line with a stated counting convention, and record the count next to each line.
Check line count against the form before deeper checks; wrong length is the first failure.
Map rhyme classes per line and compare the resulting pattern against the declared scheme.
Report every deviation with the offending line rather than a bare failure flag.
Revise the line, not the check; weakening the contract to pass is self-deception.

Storyboard Generation

Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A storyboard is the contract between a script and a shoot. The skill covers decomposing a script into shots, choosing framing and camera movement per shot, writing panel descriptions that a reviewer can verify against the script, and maintaining continuity of position, time, and screen direction across panels. Output is a numbered panel sequence with explicit per-panel specs, not prose.

When to Use

Use when a script, scene, or campaign concept must be visualized as a shot sequence for review before expensive production or animation begins.

Do not generate decorative single images and call them a storyboard. A storyboard is a numbered sequence whose continuity and screen direction can be checked panel by panel.

Inputs

Procedure
Break the script into shots; each shot gets one panel with a unique number.
For each panel, specify framing, camera movement, subject blocking, and screen direction.
Write a one-to-two sentence panel description that a reviewer can verify against the script.
Check continuity across panels: position, time of day, costume, and screen direction.
Mark transitions between panels: cut, dissolve, or move, stated explicitly.
Assemble the sequence with dialogue or action captions and export for review.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Worldbuilding

Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A fictional world breaks the moment its facts disagree: the bridge was built two centuries after the plague it preceded. This skill treats worldbuilding as a ledger — every established fact recorded once, with dates, places, and in-world sources — plus mechanical checks that new material does not contradict the record. The ledger is the artifact; prose merely cites it.

When to Use

Use when creating or extending a fictional setting — for novels, games, or campaigns — that will outlive a single writing session and must remain internally consistent.

Do not use for improvisational settings that exist for one scene; a ledger for throwaway fiction is overhead, not value.

Inputs

Procedure
Record every accepted fact exactly once with its in-world date, location, and the source that established it.
Check every draft fact against the ledger before it is accepted; contradictions are reported with both records.
Encode ordering constraints between dated events so chronology is checked mechanically, not by memory.
Prefer reconciling a contradiction over retconning silently; when a retcon is chosen, record it as a new ledger entry.
Keep the ledger versioned with the work so any chapter can be traced to the world state it was written against.
Leave gaps explicitly marked as unknown; unrecorded is not the same as unrestricted.

title: Agent Skill Security Audit
description: Audit an agent skill and its bundled resources before installation or execution, checking declared behavior, permissions, credential access, network egress, obfuscation, and sandbox requirements.
body:
Agent Skill Security Audit

Description

An agent skill is executable trust-boundary content when it contains instructions, scripts, hooks, references, or tool permissions. Audit the complete skill package before installation or execution rather than trusting its description or publisher metadata.

The audit is primarily static and compares declared behavior with the actual SKILL.md instructions and every bundled executable/resource file. Check for unexpected permission grants, credential reads, network egress, obfuscated content, hidden behavior, unsafe hooks, and mismatch between advertised and observable behavior.

Dynamic analysis is optional and must run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic or no credentials, bounded resources, controlled network access, and explicit teardown. An audit result is evidence for a trust decision; it is not a guarantee that a skill is benign.

Inputs / Outputs

Output is a structured audit record containing findings, evidence locations, severity, confidence, declared-vs-observed deltas, sandbox requirements, and a disposition such as allow, review, or deny.

Audit Procedure
Parse frontmatter and record declared name, purpose, permissions, compatibility, and provenance.
Inventory SKILL.md, scripts, hooks, binaries, configuration, references, and generated files under the skill root.
Compare advertised behavior with actual instructions and executable content.
Identify credential and sensitive-file access, including environment variables, SSH material, cloud credentials, token stores, and unrelated user data.
Identify network destinations and egress mechanisms. Treat undeclared network access as a finding requiring review.
Inspect for shell/process execution, package installation, dynamic code loading, obfuscation, encoded payloads, persistence, or attempts to hide behavior from the user.
Compare declared tool permissions with the minimum permissions required by observed behavior.
Record exact evidence locations and never treat absence of a detected pattern as proof of safety.
If dynamic analysis is required, run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic credentials, bounded resources, controlled egress, and no access to the auditor real environment.
Produce a fail-closed disposition when high-confidence critical behavior is incompatible with the declared purpose or execution policy.

Runnable Example

This example is a bounded static signal detector, not a malware detector. Production audits need language-aware analysis, archive/binary handling, symlink controls, policy evaluation, and reproducible evidence capture.

Failure Modes

Design Rules
Treat every third-party skill package as untrusted input until its behavior is reviewed.
Audit the complete package, not only SKILL.md frontmatter.
Preserve provenance and exact evidence locations for every finding.
Compare declared permissions and behavior against the least-privilege execution policy.
Default dynamic analysis to synthetic/no credentials, bounded resources, and restricted network access.
Never claim that a static scan proves a skill is safe.
Keep audit evidence separate from authorization; a passing audit does not itself grant permission to execute a skill.
Prefer deterministic checks for path, permission, secret, network, and package-integrity findings where practical.

References
OWASP Secure Agent Playbook issue #21: https://github.com/OWASP/secure-agent-playbook/issues/21
2026 research on detecting malicious agent skills: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06547
Skills Tree Sandboxed Execution: sandboxed-execution.md
Skills Tree Secret Scanning: secret-scanning.md

Container Escape Detection

Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Container isolation is a soft boundary that attackers probe before they break it. The skill covers baseline of legitimate container behavior, then watching for the escape signatures: unexpected capability use, namespace and cgroup tampering, host filesystem mounts, kernel module loading, and device node access. Detections carry the workload identity so an event can be tied to a specific deployment, not just a host.

Establish the per-workload baseline: syscalls, capabilities, mounts, and device access in normal operation.
Stream runtime events and attribute each to a workload identity and node.
Flag privileged deviations: capability escalation, namespace switching, and host path mounts.
Correlate across nodes for lateral signatures when fleet scope is enabled.
Score detections by proximity to the host boundary: what a successful escape would reach.
Emit detections with the event chain, workload identity, and containment recommendation.

body:
Dependency Integrity Verification

Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A dependency declaration names what you want; the artifact that arrives is what you run. Integrity verification closes that gap: versions pinned to exact hashes, digests recomputed at install time, signatures checked against a known identity, and provenance attestations matched to the build that produced the artifact. Anything that cannot be verified is rejected rather than installed and inspected later.

When to Use

Use before installing any third-party package in build, CI, or runtime environments — especially in automated pipelines that install without a human reading the output.

Do not treat integrity verification as vulnerability scanning: a verified artifact is exactly the reviewed bytes, which can still contain a reviewed vulnerability.

Inputs

Procedure
Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile; floating ranges bypass review by construction.
Fetch the artifact and recompute its digest locally; never trust the registry's advertised hash alone.
When a signature is available, verify it against a pinned signing identity, not a key fetched at verify time.
When provenance is available, check that the attestation's build matches the expected source and workflow.
Reject on any mismatch — digest, signature, or provenance — and fail the install.
Record the verification result (package, digest, verdict) so the decision is auditable later.

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Integrity verification proves the artifact is the one that was attested; it says nothing about the safety or quality of the code inside. Vulnerability scanning, license review, and human review remain separate, mandatory steps.

body:
Forensic Log Reconstruction

Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Incident logs never line up: clocks drift, sources overlap or gap, and formats disagree. The skill covers collecting logs from all relevant sources into an immutable evidence store, normalizing timestamps against a common clock with skew estimates, ordering events with uncertainty bounds rather than false precision, and attributing each reconstructed event to its source lines. The timeline is the deliverable, and every entry carries its evidence.

When to Use

Use when an incident must be understood from heterogeneous logs: what happened, in what order, and with what evidence supporting each claim.

Do not merge logs by raw timestamp. Clock skew between sources routinely reorders cause and effect, and a wrong order is worse than an honest uncertainty range.

Inputs

Procedure
Collect all in-scope logs into an append-only evidence store with source provenance.
Parse each source into a common event record: time, actor, action, and target.
Estimate per-source clock skew using handshake artifacts or known anchor events.
Normalize timestamps against the clock authority, carrying skew bounds as uncertainty.
Order events into a timeline, marking where uncertainty leaves the order ambiguous.
Attribute every timeline entry to its source lines so any claim can be re-verified.

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

title: Input Sanitization
description: Validate and clean every untrusted string before it reaches an LLM, a tool call, or a filesystem/SQL/HTTP boundary. Layered defense against prompt injection, SQL injection, path traversal, command injection, and PII leakage.
body:
!Dependency Status

Input Sanitization

Description

Every string that enters your agent is untrusted: user messages, tool outputs, retrieved documents, file contents, web fetches. Each one is a candidate vector for prompt injection ("ignore previous instructions"), SQL injection (), path traversal (), command injection, and data exfiltration.

This skill is the layered defense: (1) structural validation (Pydantic / JSON schema) for shape, (2) boundary-specific escaping (parameterised SQL, , ), (3) content-level analysis (PII detection, classifier, allowlist), and (4) isolation (separate LLM call to triage suspicious input). Defense is layered because any single check is bypassable.

When to Use
Any time untrusted text is going to be: (a) concatenated into a prompt, (b) passed to a tool, (c) used as a path/filename, (d) interpolated into SQL/shell.
Even when the input "comes from your database" — if it was originally typed by a user, it's untrusted.
Don't skip for "internal" tools — most prompt-injection attacks today come via retrieved documents, not the user message.

title: JWT Validation
description: Validate JSON Web Tokens by verifying the declared algorithm, signature, and claims in a fixed order so access decisions rest on cryptographic evidence instead of unverified payload strings.
body:
JWT Validation

Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A JWT is three base64url parts and a lot of trust. Skipping the verification order — algorithm, signature, then claims — is how alg=none and algorithm-confusion attacks happen. This skill defines validation as a fail-closed sequence: pin the expected algorithm, verify the signature with a constant-time comparison, then evaluate claims (expiry, audience, issuer) with an injectable clock.

When to Use

Use whenever an agent or service accepts a JWT as evidence of identity or authorization, before any decision is made on its contents.

Do not use JWTs as long-term session storage; validation is per-request evidence, and revocation needs server-side state.

Inputs

Procedure
Pin the expected algorithm in configuration; accept only that value from the token header.
Reject tokens whose header declares a different algorithm, a missing algorithm, or none — before any signature math runs.
Verify the signature over the exact signing input (header.payload) with a constant-time comparison.
Only after the signature holds, parse the payload and evaluate claims: expiry against the injected clock, audience, issuer.
Fail closed on every check; a token that fails any step is rejected without partial trust.
Log the validation outcome — verified or rejected with reason — without logging the token itself.
Never decode the payload for authorization before the signature check passes; unsigned payload is attacker input.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Token validation is the enforcement point, not the policy. A cryptographically valid token still bounds only what its claims assert: authority comes from the issuer’s policy, and every downstream action must pass its own permission checks.

Evidence

This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references:
RFC 7519 defining JSON Web Tokens (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519).
The jwt.io introduction to JWT structure and signature verification (https://jwt.io/introduction).

title: Key Rotation Automation
description: Automate cryptographic key and credential rotation across services with dual-key overlap, staged rollout, and telemetry-verified revocation, eliminating long-lived shared secrets.
body:
Key Rotation Automation

Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Rotation fails when it breaks production or when the old key survives. The skill covers inventorying keys and their dependents, rotating with dual-key overlap so consumers migrate without downtime, staging rollout by dependency order, then revoking the old key only after verifying zero usage. Every step is driven by measured telemetry, not calendar optimism.

When to Use

Use when long-lived keys and credentials must be replaced on a schedule or after exposure, across services that cannot all be updated atomically.

Do not rotate by deleting the old key and hoping. Without usage telemetry and overlap, rotation becomes an outage with a security rationale.

Inputs

Procedure
Inventory every key with its scope, dependents, and last-rotation date.
Generate the replacement and publish it alongside the old key as dual-active.
Migrate dependents in dependency order, verifying each accepts the new key.
Watch usage telemetry until the old key shows zero uses over the overlap window.
Revoke the old key and record the revocation evidence.
Alert on any key that exceeds its rotation interval or shows anomalous usage.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Rotation automation holds privileged access. Keep new keys in a secrets manager with scoped, short-lived credentials where possible, log every rotation and revocation for audit, and gate revocation on telemetry so emergency rollback remains possible.

title: Least-Privilege Scoping
description: Scope every agent action to the minimum permission set the current step needs, with deny-by-default grants, explicit expiry, and per-action audit records so lateral movement stays contained.
body:
Least-Privilege Scoping

Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A credential that can do everything will eventually do something you did not intend. Least-privilege scoping treats authorization as a narrow, expiring grant instead of ambient power: each step names the capability and resources it needs, receives exactly that, and loses it on completion. Deny-by-default evaluation, per-grant expiry, and revocation mean a compromised step can only reach what that step was already allowed to touch.

When to Use

Use when an agent or automation holds credentials that can read, write, or delete beyond the single action it is performing — tool tokens, cloud roles, or API scopes.

Do not use as a substitute for permission checks at the point of use; scoping narrows what a grant covers, and each call still needs its own decision.

Inputs

Procedure
Start from deny-by-default: an unlisted action is rejected before any tool call is attempted.
Enumerate the exact capability and resource IDs the step needs; wildcard scopes require explicit justification.
Check the request against the standing policy, then issue a grant scoped to those resources with an expiry.
Evaluate each subsequent tool call against the active grant — resource by resource, not by coarse role.
Revoke the grant at step completion, and treat any post-revocation call as a policy violation to log.
Record issued grants and their use in an audit trail that answers: who, what scope, which resources, how long.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Scoping limits what a compromised step can reach; it does not decide whether an action is correct. A perfectly scoped grant can still perform a wrong action — purpose review and destructive-action approval remain separate, human-owned checks.

Evidence

This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references:
RFC 6749 defining scoped OAuth 2.0 access (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749).
Wikipedia's overview of the principle of least privilege (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principleofleast_privilege).

MCP OAuth Authentication

Description
Authenticate a remote MCP server or agent-facing service through OAuth without embedding credentials in a skill, tool schema, repository, or generated artifact. Treat authentication and authorization as separate contracts: OAuth establishes identity/session state; authorization determines which tools and operations the agent may invoke.

When to Use
A remote MCP server requires OAuth/OIDC authentication.
Tokens rotate or expire during long-running agent sessions.
A skill must describe authentication requirements without carrying secrets.
Tool availability depends on the authenticated principal.

Inputs / Outputs

Procedure
Discover protected-resource and authorization-server metadata from authoritative configuration.
Validate redirect URI, issuer, audience/resource, PKCE requirements, and requested scopes.
Complete authorization using the approved client and user interaction boundary.
Store tokens only in the runtime credential store; never in skill files or prompts.
Before each privileged tool call, verify that the identity and granted scope authorize the operation.
On expiry or invalidation, fail closed and require the defined re-authentication path.
Record non-secret authentication evidence sufficient to diagnose failures.

Runnable Example

Failure Modes
OAuth succeeds but the MCP session exposes no authorized tools.
Stale or revoked refresh token.
Redirect URI mismatch.
Wrong audience/resource or scope.
Authentication succeeds but authorization is insufficient.
Tokens or authorization codes leak into logs or model context.

Security Boundary
OAuth does not grant permission to perform arbitrary tool actions. Tool authorization remains authoritative and must be evaluated independently.

title: Password Hashing
description: Store passwords as salted, iterated hashes with a declared cost parameter and constant-time verification so credential material is never stored in recoverable form.
body:
Password Hashing

Category: Security | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A password stored in plaintext is a breach waiting for a date; a password hashed once without salt is a rainbow-table lookup. This skill defines credential storage as a contract: a per-user random salt, a slow memory-hard or iterated hash function, a declared cost parameter, and constant-time comparison on verification. The stored record keeps the algorithm and cost with the digest so migration to stronger parameters is possible.

When to Use

Use whenever a system stores a user-provided secret for later verification — passwords, PINs, API secrets — and must never recover the plaintext.

Do not use for non-recoverable-but-high-entropy tokens like OAuth client secrets; those can be stored as plain fast hashes since entropy does the work.

Inputs

Procedure
Generate a fresh random salt per credential at first store; reuse of salts across users is a defect.
Derive the digest with a salted slow hash and a cost parameter declared in policy, never chosen per call.
Store the salt, cost, and algorithm identifier alongside the digest so verification and migration are unambiguous.
Verify by re-deriving with the stored parameters and comparing in constant time; early-exit comparison leaks timing.
Reject passwords below the declared minimum entropy policy before hashing; the hash cannot repair a weak secret.
Rehash transparently on next successful login when the policy cost rises, and record the migration.
Never log the password, its digest, or the comparison result beyond pass/fail.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Hashing protects stored credentials, not the channel or the policy: transport still needs TLS, verification still needs rate limiting, and a verified password grants only what its account’s policy allows.

Evidence

The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/PasswordStorageCheat_Sheet.html).
Wikipedia’s overview of Argon2, the winner of the Password Hashing Competition (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon2).

title: Privilege Escalation Detection
description: Detect privilege escalation attempts from authentication, authorization, and system logs by modeling normal permission change paths and flagging deviations in near real time.
body:
Privilege Escalation Detection

Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Privilege escalation rarely breaks in one step; it chains small permission wins. The skill covers modeling the legitimate paths by which accounts and processes gain privilege in an environment, then watching for events that fall outside those paths: unexpected group membership changes, service account logins on new hosts, elevation anomalies, and token manipulation. Detections are chains, so the output correlates events rather than raising single-line alerts.

When to Use

Use when authorization-relevant logs must be monitored for accounts or processes obtaining more privilege than their documented paths allow.

Do not alert on every permission change. Without a model of legitimate paths, the detection floods operators and real escalations hide in the noise.

Inputs

Procedure
Ingest authentication and authorization logs and normalize principals, actions, and targets.
Load the permission baseline: who may grant what, through which documented paths.
Match each event against the baseline; unmatched events are candidate deviations.
Correlate candidates within the window into chains: grant, use, and persist sequences.
Score chains by blast radius: what the gained privilege reaches.
Emit detections with the full chain, the baseline clause violated, and recommended response.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Escalation detections name accounts and hosts that may already be compromised. Treat detection output as need-to-know, deliver response actions through the incident process, and never auto-revoke broadly without a human confirming the chain is not a legitimate change.

Prefer native transactions when available.
Use compensating actions for irreversible external effects.

Audit both commit and rollback outcomes.
