title: Session Management
description: Create, rotate, and expire agent sessions with server-side state, opaque identifiers, and re-authentication on privilege change so identity evidence stays fresh instead of indefinitely trusted.
body:
Session Management

Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A session is a server-side record plus a token that points at it; the token is evidence, not the identity itself. Session management keeps the record authoritative: opaque identifiers, rotation on login and privilege change, idle plus absolute expiry, and invalidation that actually invalidates. A leaked old token stops working because the record moved on — not because someone hoped it would.

When to Use

Use when an agent or service maintains state across requests on behalf of an identity — web sessions, agent run sessions, or API tokens issued per engagement.

Do not use sessions as long-term authorization storage; a session says who someone was recently, and privilege should be re-established when the risk window grows.

Inputs

Procedure
Store session state server-side; issue only an opaque, high-entropy identifier to the client.
Set both idle and absolute expiry; whichever fires first ends the session.
Rotate the identifier on login, on privilege change, and on any suspected disclosure.
Invalidate the server record on logout; a client-side cookie clear is not invalidation.
Require re-authentication for sensitive operations even inside a valid session.
Record creation, rotation, and expiry events in the audit log with actor and time.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

A session carries recent identity evidence; it is not proof of continued presence or intent. Re-authentication, step-up verification, and the decision to trust a session at all remain with the identity provider and the calling service.

title: Threat Modeling
description: Model a system’s components against a structured threat taxonomy with per-interaction mitigations so security work is driven by an enumerated, reviewable threat list instead of ad-hoc paranoia.
body:
Threat Modeling

Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Security without enumeration becomes either paralysis or theater. Threat modeling imposes order: decompose the system into components and interactions, walk a fixed taxonomy — spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege — per component, and record a mitigation or an explicit acceptance for every threat found. The model is the artifact; fixes are tracked against it.

When to Use

Use when designing or changing a system that handles untrusted input, credentials, or privileged operations, and when the security posture must be explainable to a reviewer.

Do not use as a substitute for testing; a model guides where to test and review, and unverified mitigations are intentions, not protections.

Inputs

Procedure
Decompose the system into components and their interactions before naming a single threat.
Walk the declared taxonomy for every component, in a fixed order, so classes are never skipped silently.
Record each threat with its entry point and a mitigation, or an explicit accepted-risk note — never an empty cell.
Treat missing mitigations as findings with owners and deadlines, not as future hopes.
Update the model whenever the decomposition changes; a model of the old system protects nothing.
Re-test mitigations that the model claims; an untested mitigation is a documented guess.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

The model itself is sensitive: it enumerates exactly where the system is soft. Treat threat models as need-to-know artifacts and protect them with the same care as the codebase.

Vulnerability Triage

Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Triage converts a raw finding list into a fix order. The skill covers normalizing findings into a common record, scoring with a stated rubric such as CVSS adjusted for exploit maturity and asset exposure, grouping duplicates and root causes, and emitting a ranked queue with the reasoning attached. The rubric is recorded so two analysts reach the same order from the same inputs.

When to Use

Use when scanner output, penetration test findings, or external reports must be converted into a prioritized remediation queue.

Do not sort by scanner-provided severity alone. A critical on an unreachable internal host can matter less than a high on an internet-facing one, and the queue must reflect that.

Inputs

Procedure
Normalize every finding into one record: source, asset, weakness class, and evidence.
Deduplicate findings that share a root cause and link them.
Score each unique issue with the rubric: base severity, exploit maturity, and exposure.
Adjust for reachability: an issue on an unreachable host is downgraded with the reason recorded.
Group by root cause so one fix can retire multiple findings.
Emit a ranked queue with scores, rationale, and suggested fix grouping.

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Triage records are themselves sensitive: they are a map of where an organization is weak. Keep them access-controlled, share fix details on a need-to-know basis, and never expose weaponized exploit details beyond the remediation team.

title: Backpressure Handling
description: Detect and shed or buffer load when downstream consumers fall behind, using explicit queue limits, load-shedding policies, and honest propagation instead of unbounded queues.
body:
Backpressure Handling

Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Backpressure is the system admitting it is saturated instead of hiding the lag in a growing queue. The skill covers measuring consumer lag against explicit thresholds, choosing the response per queue type: bounded buffers for bursty-but-must-complete work, immediate shedding for latency-sensitive work, and degradation for work that has cheaper fallbacks. Pressure is propagated to callers honestly, because a lie here becomes a timeout there.

When to Use

Use when producers can outrun consumers: agent fleets, ingestion pipelines, or request handlers where queue growth is worse than refusal.

Do not respond to saturation with an unbounded queue. It converts a visible overload into an invisible one that eventually fails bigger and later.

Inputs

Procedure
Instrument every queue with depth and arrival and consumption rates before tuning anything.
Classify each queue: must-complete, latency-sensitive, or degradable.
Set explicit thresholds for each queue marking normal, pressured, and saturated states.
Respond by class: bounded buffer, immediate shed with a clear refusal, or degraded fallback.
Propagate pressure upstream honestly so callers can slow down instead of guessing.
Alert on sustained pressure, not transient bursts, and record shed decisions for review.

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Load shedding changes what work a system accepts, which is a policy decision with user impact. Keep shed policies in configuration with review, log what is refused, and never shed security-relevant work such as audit events or authentication under load.

title: Capability-Based Skill Selection
description: Select and sequence canonical skills for a task by matching required capabilities, discriminating competing candidates, checking eligibility and dependencies, and using execution evidence to choose the next skill.
body:
Capability-Based Skill Selection

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Capability-based skill selection turns a task into an explicit skill decision rather than treating retrieval as selection. It identifies the capabilities required by the current task, compares competing canonical skills, checks evidence, compatibility, authority, and prerequisites, then selects an executable skill and determines what should happen next from the observed result.

This skill is intended for agent runtimes and orchestrators that consume a canonical skill registry. It does not replace search, the registry, dependency graph, or execution runtime.

When to Use

Use when an agent must decide which skill to invoke for a concrete task and more than one plausible skill may match.

Do not use this as a substitute for simple deterministic lookup when the canonical skill ID is already known.

Inputs

Selection Procedure
Normalize the task into the capabilities required to make progress.
Resolve candidate skills through the canonical registry and reject unknown or non-canonical IDs.
Separate direct matches from merely related skills.
Compare competing candidates using task fit, required capability coverage, eligibility, compatibility, evidence quality, freshness, and known limitations.
Resolve mandatory prerequisites before selecting a dependent skill.
Prefer the smallest sufficient skill set; do not select skills merely because they are related.
Produce an explicit selection rationale and rejected-candidate reasons.
Invoke the selected executable skill only when its prerequisites and authority conditions are satisfied.
Verify the result against the task acceptance criteria.
If verification fails, classify the failure and select the next justified skill or recovery action rather than blindly repeating the same invocation.
Stop when the task is verified complete, blocked by an external condition, or requires escalation.

Outputs

Decision Contract

A valid selection must answer all of these questions:
What capability is required now?
Which canonical skill satisfies it?
Why is it better than the competing candidates?
Which prerequisites must run first?
Is the skill eligible in the current context?
What evidence will verify the invocation?
What result causes the agent to invoke the next skill?
What result causes recovery, substitution, escalation, or termination?

A skill must not be selected solely because it contains matching keywords.

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Skill selection does not grant permissions. The selected skill must execute only within its declared authority, security boundary, compatibility constraints, and available runtime permissions.

High-impact or irreversible actions must remain subject to the governing approval and policy controls of the consuming agent runtime.

Public demand signals around automated task breakdown, agent orchestration, and assignment based on skills/performance.

title: Circuit Breaking
description: Stop calling a failing dependency after a threshold, fail fast while the circuit is open, and probe with trial calls before closing so one slow or broken service cannot take the caller down with it.
body:
Circuit Breaking

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Retries have a limit beyond which they become part of the outage. A circuit breaker converts persistent failure into a fast, local decision: after a threshold of consecutive failures the circuit opens and calls short-circuit immediately; after a reset window a limited probe tests the water; only a successful probe closes the circuit again. The caller sheds load and stays responsive while the dependency recovers.

When to Use

Use around any remote dependency whose failure or latency can exhaust the caller — model APIs, databases, downstream services called on a request path.

Do not wrap workloads where every call must succeed; a breaker that skips required work turns degraded mode into silent data loss.

Inputs

Procedure
Track consecutive failures per dependency, not globally; one bad endpoint should not open every circuit.
When the count reaches the threshold, open the circuit and fail fast — no call, no queue, no waiting.
While open, answer immediately with a defined degradation result, never with an exception shape callers have not agreed to.
After the reset timeout, move to half-open and allow exactly one probe call; the rest still fail fast.
Close on a successful probe and reset the counter; re-open and restart the timer on a failed probe.
Export circuit state as a metric; state transitions are the outage narrative.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

The breaker protects the caller's time and threads; it does not repair the dependency or verify its recovery. Post-incident validation of the dependency stays with its owner, and an open circuit is a degraded state, never a healthy one.

Evidence

title: Cross-Agent Locking
description: Coordinate exclusive access to shared resources across distributed agents using leases with fencing tokens, preventing deadlocks and torn writes from concurrent mutation.
body:
Cross-Agent Locking

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

When two agents can mutate the same resource, correctness needs a lock, and distributed locks need more than mutual exclusion. The skill covers choosing lock granularity, issuing time-bounded leases with fencing tokens so a stalled holder cannot corrupt later writers, ordering acquisition to prevent deadlock, and handling the crash case: leases expire, the next holder proceeds, and the fencing token rejects the zombie. Lock state lives in a coordinator both sides can see, never in agent memory.

When to Use

Use when multiple agents operate on shared state or resources that must not be mutated concurrently: shared files, external accounts, or single-instance workflows.

Do not treat advisory flags in a shared document as locks. Without a coordinator, expiry, and fencing, two agents will both believe they hold the resource.

Inputs

Procedure
Choose lock granularity: the smallest scope that prevents the conflict, not the whole task.
Acquire a lease from the coordinator with a bounded TTL and a fencing token number.
Record the token with every mutation so stale writes can be rejected downstream.
Acquire multiple locks in a fixed global order to prevent deadlock cycles.
Release the lease immediately after the critical section; never hold across waits.
Handle expiry: renew in-flight if needed, and accept rejection when a higher token exists.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Lock coordinators become shared infrastructure with availability impact. Authenticate lease acquisition, scope tokens to the resource, and audit the acquisition log, because the log is the evidence in any post-incident dispute over who held what.

description: Route repeatedly failing messages to a dedicated dead-letter queue with full failure metadata so poison payloads are quarantined for inspection instead of blocking the pipeline or vanishing.
body:
Dead-Letter Queuing

Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Some messages cannot be processed, and retrying them forever converts one bad payload into a stuck pipeline. Dead-letter queuing draws the line: after a bounded number of attempts, the message moves to a dedicated dead-letter queue carrying its attempts, errors, and original payload. The main queue keeps flowing, the failure stays inspectable, and a replay path exists for after the cause is fixed.

When to Use

Use with any task queue or event pipeline where a malformed or failing message must not block subsequent messages.

Do not use a dead-letter queue as a trash bin: entries are quarantined pending diagnosis, and unbounded growth without review hides an outage in plain sight.

Inputs

Procedure
Track attempts per message id; the count travels with the message, not with worker memory.
On each failure, record the error and timestamp; retry only while under the attempt bound.
At the bound, move the message to the dead-letter queue with its payload, attempts, and error history attached.
Surface dead-letter depth and entry age as operational alarms; a growing dead-letter queue is a failing pipeline.
Diagnose entries before replay: fix the consumer or correct the payload, then replay deliberately.
Re-run replayed messages through the same accounting so a still-failing replay dead-letters again, visibly.

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

The dead-letter queue quarantines and preserves; it does not diagnose. Root-cause analysis, payload correction, and the decision to replay remain operator work, with the quarantine treated as evidence, not as a fix.

title: Deadline Propagation
description: Carry one absolute end-time deadline through every orchestration hop so each step budgets its remaining time, children inherit a tightened deadline, and late results are discarded rather than delivered.
body:
Deadline Propagation

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Relative timeouts do not compose: three sequential steps with a 5-second timeout each can stall a caller for 15 seconds. Deadline propagation fixes the arithmetic by carrying one absolute end time: each hop computes remaining time against the same clock, children receive the tighter of their own budget and the parent's remaining time, and results that arrive after the deadline are discarded instead of patched into the run late.

When to Use

Use in any multi-hop orchestration — service calls, subagent trees, pipelines — where a caller's total wait must stay bounded.

Do not substitute per-hop timeouts without checking the sum; a chain of local limits is not a global one.

Inputs

Procedure
Set one absolute deadline at run start, from the caller's wall-clock budget; it is a timestamp, not a duration.
At each hop, compute remaining time as deadline minus now; a hop with no remaining time fails fast without starting.
Give each child the tighter of its own budget and the parent's remaining time minus the parent's reserve.
Reject late results even if they eventually complete; a result after the deadline is not a result for this run.
Record per-step time consumption so postmortems can show where the budget went.
Reserve a margin for serialization and cleanup; a deadline with no reserve fails at the packaging step.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Deadline propagation bounds wall-clock time; it does not certify the quality of what was rushed to fit. Quality gates, evaluation, and review apply the same standards regardless of how much budget a step had.

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Replication turns local state into a survivable one. The skill covers choosing a consistency model appropriate to the workload, serializing state with deterministic ordering, replicating with quorum acknowledgment before declaring a write durable, and merging concurrent updates with a deterministic rule so all replicas converge without a human referee. Define the state object and its write paths before choosing replication mechanics.
Choose the consistency model and the ordering authority: a leader or a quorum rule.
Serialize updates with a deterministic order: sequence numbers or version vectors, never wall clocks.
Replicate each update and declare durability only after quorum acknowledgment.
Merge concurrent updates with a deterministic conflict rule so replicas converge.
Recover failed workers by rebuilding their state from the acknowledged replica log.

body:
Dynamic Team Formation

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Not every task deserves a team. The skill covers deciding when a single agent suffices, deriving required roles from the task decomposition, selecting agents by declared capability rather than identity, writing per-role contracts with inputs, outputs, and authority limits, and sizing the team against a budget. Teams disband on completion with artifacts returned, because lingering agents are cost and confusion.

When to Use

Use when a task decomposes into heterogeneous subtasks that benefit from specialists working in parallel or in sequence within one run.

Do not spawn a full team for every task. Larger teams pay communication overhead that simple tasks cannot amortize, and unnecessary agents multiply cost and failure surface.

Inputs

Procedure
Decide whether the task needs a team at all: single-agent unless decomposition shows real heterogeneity.
Derive required roles from the subtasks, one role per distinct capability cluster.
Select agents by declared capability fit, recording the second choice for each role.
Write per-role contracts: inputs, outputs, authority limits, and escalation path.
Size the team against the budget, trading concurrency against cost per unit of work.
Disband on completion, returning artifacts and freeing capacity explicitly.

Security and Authority Boundary

Dynamically formed teams can expand the blast radius of a compromised member. Scope each agent to the minimum authorities its role contract needs, audit capability declarations in the registry, and never allow formation logic to grant authority it cannot revoke.

title: Evidence Verification
description: Verify meaningful repository changes with direct implementation, test, CI, and documentation evidence.
body:
Evidence Verification

Description

Verify completion claims against direct repository, test, CI, security, and documentation evidence. Separate verified facts from assumptions and unresolved risks.
Identify the claim being verified and its strongest evidence source.
Inspect the actual changed implementation.
Execute or inspect required validation gates.
Verify the resulting main commit and relevant CI runs.
Check security implications and documentation synchronization.
Report verified facts separately from unresolved risks and assumptions.
Use the precise completion states defined by AGENTS.md.

Runnable example

Inputs / outputs / failure modes

Failure Modes
Evidence substitution: accepting an adjacent artifact (a passing CI run for a different commit, a related document) as proof of the actual claim; match evidence to the exact claim, commit, and artifact.
Assumption laundering: classifying inferred or reported facts as "verified" without a direct artifact; keep verified, assumed, and unresolved strictly separated.
Incomplete evidence matrix: verifying positive claims but not absence claims (no regression, no unresolved risk); negative claims need named evidence too.
Stale evidence: reusing evidence collected before a change that could invalidate it; timestamp and re-check evidence at verification time.

title: Idempotency Keys
description: Assign client-generated idempotency keys to state-changing requests so retries and at-least-once delivery produce one effect, with duplicate calls returning the recorded first result.
body:
Idempotency Keys

Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

At-least-once delivery means the same request will sometimes arrive twice; idempotency keys turn that from a bug into a non-event. The client attaches a unique key to each operation intent, the server checks the key before executing, and a replayed key returns the stored first response instead of executing again. The stored response plus a payload fingerprint closes the gap between "same key" and "same request".

When to Use

Use for any state-changing request that may be retried — payment calls, task creation, webhook handlers, queue consumers under at-least-once semantics.

Do not bother for pure reads or naturally idempotent operations; the machinery earns its cost only where duplicates have effects.

Inputs

Procedure
Generate the key client-side, unique per operation intent — not per session, not per process.
Before executing, look the key up: a hit with a matching fingerprint returns the stored response; a hit with a mismatching fingerprint is an error.
On a miss, execute once, then store the response keyed by the key and fingerprint.
Keep the TTL at least as long as the client's longest retry window; shorter expiry quietly reintroduces duplicates.
Keep keys out of URLs and logs; they identify operations and may correlate to sensitive intents.
Treat in-flight keys as locked: concurrent duplicate calls wait for the first execution rather than racing it.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Idempotency protects the server's effect from duplication; it does not order distinct operations. Sequencing two different calls — even related ones — needs explicit ordering, which this skill does not provide.

Evidence

Stripe's API documentation on idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests).

title: Kanban Task Management
description: Maintain a persistent, file-backed Kanban board as the shared source of task truth between a coding agent, its orchestrator, and a human reviewer: an explicit task lifecycle with receipted transitions, a blocked-by dependency DAG with a derived ready set, and a per-task merge gate whose completion evidence is verified before a task may be marked done.
body:
Category: Orchestration
Skill Level: Intermediate
Stability: experimental
Version: v1
Added: 2026-10
Last Updated: 2026-10

Description

Kanban task management gives an agent a durable board it can read and mutate between sessions instead of holding the plan in context. The board is plain files under version control in the repository being worked, so task state survives crashes, context resets, and handoffs between agents and humans. This page defines a portable contract for lifecycle, dependencies, concurrency, and completion evidence; concrete implementations are references, not requirements.

The Portable Contract

Any conforming implementation must provide:
Board store: task records stored as files inside the repository (or a directory the repository's review surface can see). Never a side-channel database a code review cannot diff.
Task record: stable ID, status, summary, tags,  edges (referencing other task IDs), an append-only list of transition receipts, and evidence references (commit SHAs, merge receipts).
Transition receipts: every status change must append a receipt (timestamp, old→new status, human-readable response message, optional evidence). Receipts are never rewritten or deleted.
Controller CLI: the only writer. Mutations happen through controller commands; direct hand-edits of board files are out-of-contract (see Concurrency Model).
Derived ready set: a query that returns, without mutating anything, the tasks an agent may legally pick up next (status eligible and all  targets satisfied per the semantics below).

Task Lifecycle: Legal and Illegal Transitions

States: , plus  (soft, orthogonal) and  (a flag on , not a fifth state).

Setting/clearing the  flag on  is always legal with a receipt; a blocked task leaves the ready set until cleared.

Blocked-By Dependency Semantics

Edges are validated at write time and re-validated by every ready-set computation:

The ready set is always recomputed from the live DAG — cached orderings are never trusted.

Concurrency Model

Read-before-mutate is not concurrency control: two agents can both read the same state and then both write, losing one transition. The contract prescribes exactly one of:
Single controller: one controller process owns the board and serializes mutations, or
Optimistic CAS: every mutation carries the content hash of the board state it was computed against; on mismatch the controller aborts and the agent re-reads.

Hand-edited board files are detected as drift and must be reconciled through the controller.

Completion Evidence

Implementations may declare a completion gate per task:

A  gate must verify the repository's actual merge state. Reopening a completed task creates a new evidence cycle and never rewrites Git history.

title: Result Aggregation
description: Collect parallel task results into one ordered report with per-task status, explicit handling of failures and stragglers, and deterministic merge order so the combined output stays reproducible.
body:
Result Aggregation

Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Parallel execution multiplies results and failure shapes at the same time. Aggregation turns a cloud of futures into one report: each task contributes a (id, status, output) tuple, missing tasks appear as missing instead of vanishing, and the merge order is deterministic. The aggregate carries per-task provenance, so any claim in the combined output can be traced back to the task that produced it.

When to Use

Use whenever work is split across parallel subagents or workers and the caller needs one combined, trustworthy answer.

Do not use unordered ad-hoc merging; a merge that depends on arrival order produces a different output on every run.

Inputs

Procedure
Register the full expected task id set at dispatch time; the plan, not the arrival count, defines completeness.
Collect results as (id, status, output) tuples; failures are results, not exceptions to swallow.
On aggregation, subtract completed ids from expected ids; anything unaccounted is missing — with the timeout recorded.
Apply the merge policy per status: include completed, record failed, mark missing; the policy decides what missing means for the whole.
Merge in task id order, never arrival order, so identical inputs produce identical output.
Emit the aggregate with per-task provenance: which task produced which part of the combined result.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Aggregation preserves and reports what subagents returned; it cannot judge whether the content is correct. Validation of merged content — sources, calculations, claims — remains a separate, explicit step.

body:
Speculative Execution

Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Speculation buys latency with resources. The skill covers choosing which steps are worth speculating, defining acceptance criteria per path before launch, launching redundant candidates against independent resources, taking the first result that passes the criteria, and cancelling the losers. Because duplicated work multiplies cost and side effects, every speculative path must be idempotent and side-effect-free until acceptance.

When to Use

Use when a step is both slow and uncertain: slow model calls, flaky external services, or retrieval where any of several paths can satisfy the caller.

Do not speculate on steps with external side effects before acceptance. Two accepted writes is a correctness bug that costs more than the latency saved.

Inputs

Procedure
Confirm the step is worth speculating: latency saved must exceed added resource cost.
Write acceptance criteria before launching anything, including how the winner is judged.
Verify every candidate path is idempotent and free of external side effects before acceptance.
Launch candidates concurrently against independent resources to avoid correlated failure.
Take the first result that passes acceptance and cancel the losers immediately.
Record per-path outcomes and cost so the speculation decision can be audited and retuned.

Speculation multiplies external calls, which multiplies exposure to rate limits and data egress. Scope candidate paths to the least privilege needed, do not speculate across security boundaries where one path has wider authority than the task requires, and audit cancelled paths for partial writes.

title: Workflow Versioning
description: Version workflow definitions explicitly and record the version in every execution so in-flight runs keep a stable identity while definitions evolve without silent breakage.
body:
Workflow Versioning

Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A workflow definition is code that runs many times. Versioning it explicitly — semantic bumps, a recorded version per execution, and a written rule for what counts as compatible — separates "the run behaved as defined" from "the definition changed underneath the run". Executions carry their definition version, so a result can always be traced to the exact steps that produced it.

When to Use

Use whenever a multi-step workflow runs repeatedly and its steps, prompts, tool wiring, or output schema may change over time.

Do not use one mutable definition with in-place edits; every execution should be able to name the version that produced it.

Inputs

Procedure
Assign each definition an explicit version; an unversioned definition is a defect, not a default.
Classify every change against the written rule: step removal, output schema change, or semantic edits are breaking; additive steps are additive; wording fixes are fixes.
Record the definition version inside every execution at start; a result without a version cannot be interpreted later.
Pin in-flight executions to the version they started with; migrate only between runs, never during one.
For breaking bumps, provide an explicit migration or a compatibility window; never change a version in place.
Keep the definition history queryable so any past result can be replayed against its own version.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Versioning preserves the structure of orchestration; it does not pin model behavior. Two executions of the same version can still differ from model sampling — output reproducibility needs seed, prompt, and model tracking of its own.

description: Order learning units into a dependency-respecting path — prerequisites as edges, cycle detection, mastery gates — so study plans stay coherent, individually paced, and free of impossible orders.
body:
Curriculum Sequencing

Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A curriculum is a directed graph wearing a reading list's clothes. Sequencing it means extracting prerequisite edges from stated dependencies, verifying the graph is acyclic, ordering units topologically, and placing mastery gates between a unit and everything that depends on it. Placement tests adjust the entry point by skipping proven material — not by deleting it, since a skipped unit must remain visible in the path's record.

When to Use

Use when a set of lessons, modules, or skills must be ordered for a learner — course assembly, onboarding plans, or personalized study paths.

Do not use for a flat list with no real dependencies; sorting adds ceremony without value when the graph has no edges.

Inputs

Procedure
Extract prerequisite edges exactly as stated; an assumed-but-unstated dependency is an edge nobody can audit.
Detect cycles first; a cyclic curriculum has no valid order, only a hidden wrong edge to fix.
Produce a topological order of the units; ties break deterministically (by unit id) for reproducible plans.
Apply placement: units already mastered are marked skipped-in-place, never removed from the record.
Insert mastery gates before dependents: a unit's dependents unlock only when its gate is passed.
Emit the path with per-unit status (assigned, skipped, gated) and the edge set it was derived from.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Sequencing orders material; it certifies nothing about mastery. What a completed path means is decided by assessment quality, which this skill consumes but does not provide.

Energy Consumption Forecasting

Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Load forecasting is regular until it is not. The skill covers building the baseline from calendar and weather effects, adding autoregressive load structure, handling regime changes such as holidays and extreme events, and reporting forecasts with error bands calibrated on backtests rather than assumed. Clean the load history: gaps, daylight-saving transitions, and meter rollovers handled explicitly.
Engineer calendar and weather features: hour, weekday, holiday, heating and cooling degrees.
Fit the baseline and autoregressive components on training data only.
Backtest on held-out recent periods and calibrate error bands from realized residuals.
Adjust for regime days, such as holidays and extreme weather, with dedicated handling.
Publish the forecast with intervals and the regime assumptions it depends on.

description: Compute reorder points and order quantities from demand history, lead time, and safety stock with every formula input recorded so replenishment decisions rest on stated math rather than gut feel.
body:
Inventory Reordering

Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Reordering is arithmetic pretending to be intuition. The skill makes the math explicit: demand statistics from history, a reorder point from demand rate times lead time plus safety stock, an order quantity from policy (economic order quantity or a stated rule), and a comparison against stock on hand that emits a concrete reorder list. Every input — history window, lead time, service level — is recorded with the decision, so the same numbers regenerate the same order.

When to Use

Use for any stocked item where running out has a cost and overstocking has another — spare parts, consumables, retail or warehouse inventory.

Do not use on sparse or stale demand history; a reorder point computed from three data points is a guess with extra decimals.

Inputs

Procedure
Fix the history window and clean the series — stockouts and promotions are noted, not silently averaged in.
Compute demand rate and variability; record the window and both statistics with the decision.
Compute the reorder point as demand rate times lead time plus safety stock, from the recorded inputs only.
Derive the order quantity from the stated policy — economic order quantity or a rule — with its formula and inputs recorded.
Compare stock on hand against the reorder point; items at or below it enter the reorder list with the computed quantity.
Emit the decision record: item, inputs, formulas, quantities, and date, so the order is reproducible.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Reordering math supports the operational decision; supplier risk, cash constraints, and contract terms remain with procurement. A computed quantity is a recommendation with provenance, not a purchase order.

title: Receipt Parsing
description: Extract merchant, date, line item, tax, and total fields from raw receipt text with arithmetic cross-checks so expense records rest on validated numbers rather than best guesses.
body:
Receipt Parsing

Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A receipt is unstructured text pretending to be a table. Parsing it means segmentation (header, items, totals), normalization (dates, currencies, decimal separators per locale), and — the part that separates data from guesswork — arithmetic verification: line items must sum to the subtotal, and subtotal plus tax must match the stated total. Every extracted field carries its raw span, so any number in the structured record can be traced to where it came from.

When to Use

Use when receipt text (typed or OCR output) must become structured expense data — bookkeeping automation, reimbursement workflows, spend analysis.

Do not use when a structured source exists instead; supplier invoices with structured input are a stricter field contract handled by invoice processing.

Inputs

Procedure
Segment the text: header block, line-item block, totals block; totals are parsed from the bottom up, where receipts are most structured.
Normalize numbers per locale — decimal separator, currency symbol, thousands grouping — before any arithmetic.
Parse line items as (quantity, description, amount) triples; wrapped descriptions are joined, not split into items.
Cross-check: item sum against stated subtotal; subtotal plus tax against stated total; record the verdict per check.
When a stated total is missing, compute it and flag it as computed, never as extracted.
Output the structured record with per-field raw spans and confidence; unresolved fields are flagged, not invented.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Parsed receipts are structured data for review, not financial records of record. Reimbursement approval, tax treatment, and fraud detection remain with the accounting workflow and its human checks.

description: Screen resumes against a written rubric with per-criterion evidence spans, anchored scoring, and explicit missing-information handling so ranking decisions stay auditable and bias-controlled.
body:
Resume Screening

Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Resume screening is a judgment task wrapped in an audit problem. The skill makes the judgment mechanical and the audit trivial: criteria are written before any resume is read, each criterion is scored only against quoted evidence from the document, missing information is recorded as missing rather than punished, and protected attributes are never inferred or used. The output is a structured verdict with provenance, not a ranking by feel.

When to Use

Use when a stack of resumes must be reduced to a ranked or triaged shortlist against a defined role, and the decision must be explainable afterward.

Do not use to make hiring decisions; screening output is decision support that humans review before any candidate outcome.

Inputs

Procedure
Fix the rubric before reading resumes; criteria written after reading a candidate are advocacy, not screening.
For each criterion, quote the evidence span from the resume that supports a score, or record it as missing.
Score against anchored levels defined in the rubric; two screeners should reach the same score from the same span.
Treat missing information as missing — a gap is not a negative unless the rubric says so explicitly.
Never infer protected attributes from text, dates, or names; they are out of scope by construction.
Emit the structured verdict with every span, score, and gap, so the decision can be reconstructed or challenged.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Shift Scheduling

Category: Domain-Specific | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A roster is a set of assignments that satisfies stated constraints — or it is a wish. This skill treats scheduling as constraint programming: enumerate shifts and coverage requirements, encode hard constraints (availability, max hours, minimum rest between shifts) and soft ones (fairness in weekends and unpopular shifts), search for a feasible assignment, and report every constraint that could not be satisfied rather than quietly producing a broken roster.

When to Use

Use for on-call rotations, support coverage, clinical or retail staffing — any recurring horizon where people must be assigned to shifts under rules.

Do not use for one-off task allocation with no recurring structure or constraints; that is task assignment, not scheduling.

Inputs

Procedure
Enumerate the shift grid across the horizon; every slot that needs coverage appears in the problem.
Encode hard constraints first — availability, maximum hours, minimum rest gaps; soft constraints carry explicit priorities.
Search for a feasible assignment; prefer solutions that minimize weighted soft-constraint violations.
When no feasible roster exists, report which constraints conflict and at which slots — do not silently drop coverage.
Compute fairness per person (shift counts, weekends, unpopular slots) and include it in the output.
On any later edit, revalidate the full roster; an edited roster is a new solution, not an exception to check.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

A feasible schedule satisfies the stated constraints; labor-law compliance depends on those constraints being complete and current. Human approval of the published roster — and of constraint changes — remains mandatory.

title: Alerting Design
description: Build alerts around user-visible symptoms and service objectives rather than raw causes, so a page means real impact and silence means real health.
body:
Alerting Design

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

An alert on every metric is a pager that cannot be trusted, and a pager that cannot be trusted gets silenced — usually right before the one that mattered. This skill designs alerting from the top down: start from what users experience, define objectives with error budgets, and alert on the burn rate of those budgets. Cause-level signals become dashboards and debug entries, not pages, because a page is a claim that a human must act now, and every unactionable claim spends trust the system needs for the real ones.

When to Use

Use whenever a service is on call — user-facing or internal — and especially where pages have grown noisy enough that responders pre-filter them.

Do not page on individual cause metrics with no user-visible symptom; a nearly full disk at three in the morning is a dashboard, not a human.

Inputs

Procedure
Define the objective first — what users experience, measured as availability or latency — before writing a single alert.
Alert on burn rate: page when the error budget would exhaust within a bounded window, not on any single bad sample.
Keep causes out of the pager: route saturation and dependency signals to dashboards and debug pages, not to humans.
Make every page actionable: name the runbook, the owner, and the first command to run, in the alert itself.
Review alert performance like code: page rate, action rate, and the fraction of pages that were real become metrics.
Retire or repair chatty alerts immediately; a noisy alert is not a safety margin, it is a removed one.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Alert content travels to the widest, least protected channel in an organization — phones and chat: alert payloads must not embed credentials, internal topology details, or user data, and access to the alerting configuration itself must be protected, because silencing rules are a prime target for an intruder who wants the quiet path.

title: Blue-Green Deployment
description: Run two production environments and switch traffic between them, so a release becomes a reversible routing change instead of a waiting period for breakage.
body:
Blue-Green Deployment

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A deployment that mutates the live environment in place makes rollback a race against the damage. This skill keeps two full environments — blue, live, and green, idle — and makes the release a routing flip: the new version deploys to the idle color, is verified there, traffic switches to it, and the old color stays warm for exactly as long as the new one needs to prove itself. Rollback is then the same switch in the other direction, which is what makes the flip a decision rather than a gamble.

When to Use

Use for stateless or forward-compatible services where a full second environment is affordable and a fast, reversible cutover is worth the cost.

Do not blue-green around breaking database changes: if the old color cannot run on the new schema, the switch is not reversible and the pattern is theater.

Inputs

Procedure
Keep two environments, with the idle one always ready to receive the next release.
Deploy the new version to the idle color only, and verify it there — health, smoke, readiness — while production is untouched.
Flip routing to the new color, gradually or at once by design, and watch the user-visible symptoms rather than the deploy logs.
Keep the old color warm for the soak period: rollback during soak is a routing change, measured in seconds.
Handle state carefully: the schema and its consumers must be forward-compatible with both colors, or the flip is one-way.
Retire the old version after soak, and immediately prepare the idle color for the next release — the pattern only works while it is always two environments.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

The routing switch is a security boundary: whoever can flip traffic between environments can redirect production, so route changes require the same authorization and audit as production deploys, and the idle environment must hold production data protections even while idle.

Capacity Planning

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Define growth scenarios explicitly: trend, step events, and their probabilities.
Project demand per scenario over the planning horizon.
Derive required capacity per scenario against the target ceilings.

body:
Container Image Tagging

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A tag is a label someone can move; a digest is an identity they cannot. This skill pins that difference into the pipeline: builds get version tags once, deployments reference images by digest, a tag is never reassigned to different bytes, and every artifact carries build provenance — source commit, build definition, timestamp. The result is that any deployed environment can answer "exactly which bytes are running, and where did they come from".

When to Use

Use for any container image that reaches a deployment — application services, tooling images, CI runner environments.

Do not deploy floating tags such as  or a bare branch name; a deployment that cannot name its bytes cannot be rolled back to them either.

Inputs

Procedure
Build once per version; the artifact from one build receives all its tags at creation time.
Tag with the semantic version; tags are claims about content, applied once and never retagged.
Record the registry digest; deployments pin by digest, with the version tag kept for humans.
Attach provenance to the artifact — source commit, build definition, build time — as metadata or attestation.
Reject retag requests: a tag that points at new bytes is a new version, whatever it is called.
Keep tag-to-digest mappings queryable so an environment's running bytes can be resolved historically.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Tagging identifies artifacts; it does not make them safe. Vulnerability scanning and signature verification are separate steps whose verdicts attach to the digest, not to the label.

Database Backup Automation

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. The skill covers scheduling full and incremental backups with a retention policy that survives audit, encrypting and off-siting them, and, decisively, restoring on a schedule into an isolated environment to verify the backup is complete, current, and usable. Encrypt backups at rest and in transit, and copy them off-site per policy.
Prune expired backups per retention tiers and log what was removed.
Restore on schedule into the isolated environment and verify completeness and usability.
Report measured recovery time against the objective and alert on drift.

Security and Authority Boundary

Declarative Infrastructure

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Infrastructure described imperatively is infrastructure nobody can rebuild: the console clicks that made it exist live in a browser history. This skill makes the desired state the source of truth: resources are declared in code, the code is reviewed and versioned, and a reconciler applies the declaration — reporting a diff between what exists and what is wanted before it changes anything. The payoff is that the environment is no longer a memory; it is a file, with a history, that can be recreated in another region on a bad day.

When to Use

Use for any environment expected to outlive a single change — clusters, databases, networks, queues — and for anything that must be rebuilt identically elsewhere.

Do not drive one-off break-glass resources through the declarative pipeline during an incident; make the manual change, record it, and reconcile the declaration afterward.

Inputs

Procedure
Declare desired state in code — resources, parameters, and their relations — with nothing that exists only as a console change.
Store the declaration in version control with review, so every infrastructure change has an author, a diff, and a reason.
Preview before applying: generate the plan and read it, because the apply step is where the diff meets production.
Apply through the reconciler, and let it record state — never mutate resources by hand where the controller watches them.
Treat drift as an incident: a manual change to a managed resource gets reconciled or recorded, not ignored.
Rehearse the rebuild: a declaration that has never created a fresh environment is a hypothesis, not a backup.

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Infrastructure code holds the shape of the estate and often the references to its most sensitive stores: declarations must be reviewed with the same scrutiny as application code, secrets referenced by identity rather than embedded, and reconciler credentials guarded as the master key to every resource it can create.

title: Dependency Auditor
description: Audit declared skill dependencies and executable examples in isolated environments, producing reproducible pass/fail evidence without silently promoting trust state.
body:
!Dependency Status

Dependency Auditor

Description

Audit declared external dependencies and executable skill examples in isolated environments. The auditor records pass/fail evidence and proposes badge artifacts without directly changing canonical trust state.

Phase 3 of the Dependency Watchdog pipeline.
Closes the gap between Package Exists (🟡 Yellow) and Code Runs (🟢 Green).

The Execution Gap

The AST Sweep (Phase 1) confirms that a skill's declared packages exist on PyPI
and are free of known CVEs. But existence ≠ execution. A package might:
Have breaking API changes in its latest release
Require a native system dependency (e.g. , ) absent from the runner
Conflict with another skill's dependencies when installed together
Simply have a typo in its import path in the code example

The Dependency Auditor solves this by running the code, not just scanning it.

Architecture

Isolation Strategy

Each skill runs in a completely independent virtual environment.
This prevents dependency bleed between skills — Skill A's 
cannot shadow Skill B's .

Why not a single shared venv for all skills?
Because conflicts between skill deps would produce false results.
Skill A might pass only because Skill B's dep happened to satisfy its import.
Isolation ensures every Green badge is independently earned.

Verdict Logic

The auditor distinguishes three outcomes. The distinction between  and 
is the single most important design decision — it keeps the CI signal clean.

The Human-in-the-Loop Contract

The badge is not written directly into canonical skill content. A passing audit produces a proposed badge artifact on a new branch and opens a Pull Request. The exact PR HEAD is merged only when required repository CI, security, tests, and invariants pass.

This is the critical security feature. Without it, a snippet that passes due
to a flaky network call or a temporary PyPI outage could silently award a
Green badge that isn't earned.

Recursive Dogfooding

This skill () is itself subject to the badge pipeline it describes.
Its own  and  imports are scanned by the AST Sweep → Yellow badge
The Dependency Auditor runs its own snippets in an isolated venv
If they pass → a verification PR is opened → exact-head repository CI gates the merge → Green badge

The tool that audits the repository is itself audited by the repository.
This is the self-healing property of the infrastructure.

Security: Network Constraint Model

See  for the full threat model.

The short version:

For the current scope — a curated, maintainer-reviewed repository — the
ephemeral runner model is the primary and sufficient containment strategy.

Failure Modes
Verdict overreach: recording pass/fail evidence as a trust judgment; the auditor records evidence and proposes badges, it does not change canonical trust state.
Isolation leakage: network or filesystem egress from the audit environment beyond the documented constraint model invalidates that run's evidence.
Pinned-evidence drift: verdicts referencing dependency versions that no longer match the resolved lockfile at audit time; record the exact resolved versions.
Transitive blind spots: auditing declared dependencies only while the exploitable surface lives in transitive or undeclared (phantom) dependencies.
Stale advisories: advisory databases with lagging or missing entries producing false "no known issues" verdicts; record advisory database version and freshness.

Related Infrastructure

Evidence
The canonical skill file is the authoritative repository implementation. Repository schema, validation workflows, and the Agent Skills projection contract define structural conformance. Implementation guidance must remain traceable to supplied or independently verified authoritative sources; no benchmark claim is made without reproducible evidence.

Deployment Rollback

Category: Infrastructure | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Rollback is a deployment you have already practiced — or a hope. The skill makes it an artifact: the previous release stays deployable, schema migrations carry their compensating steps, the rollback procedure is rehearsed in staging against the same artifact shape, and recovery runs in a defined order with health verification at the end. Rehearse the rollback in staging with the same artifacts and order; an unrehearsed plan is a draft.
On the failure signal, execute in the recorded order: stop traffic, revert code, revert migrations step by step, restore configuration.
Verify health after rollback — probes, smoke checks, error rates — before declaring recovery.
Write the incident reference: trigger, release delta, migration state, recovery time against budget.

DNS Record Management

Category: Infrastructure | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

DNS is the first link in every request path, and its failure modes are slow and confusing. The skill covers expressing records as versioned configuration, choosing TTLs deliberately as a trade between change speed and resolver load, pre-validating changes against the existing zone, applying with a rollback plan, and verifying propagation from independent resolvers rather than assuming it. Record changes follow production discipline because a mistake here takes down everything.

When to Use

Use when zones and records must be created, modified, or migrated, or when DNS changes need controlled rollout and verification.

Do not lower a TTL and change the record in the same step. The sequence is: lower the TTL, wait out the old TTL, then change the record.

Inputs

Procedure
Fetch the current zone state from the authoritative source and record it as the rollback point.
Validate the change set: conflicting records, CNAME exclusivity, and target reachability.
Apply the TTL strategy: lower before risky changes, restore after verification.
Apply changes in dependency order, with service-critical records last when migration allows.
Verify propagation from independent resolvers until all answer consistently.
Archive the applied state and confirm monitoring reflects the new topology.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

DNS control is domain control: a compromised zone can redirect every service, including login flows. Keep zone configuration in version control with review, restrict API credentials tightly, enable change auditing, and treat delegation changes with the same care as certificate authority changes.

title: Health Check Endpoints
description: Expose separate liveness and readiness endpoints with dependency-aware checks so orchestrators restart dead processes while temporarily unready ones simply receive no traffic.
body:
Health Check Endpoints

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

Liveness answers "is this process broken"; readiness answers "can it serve right now". Conflating them produces the two classic outages: restarts during a dependency blip (the process is fine, the database is not) and traffic routed to instances that cannot serve. This skill splits the endpoints, makes readiness check real dependencies with real timeouts, and degrades to unready instead of dead — because a restart loop solves nothing a moment of patience would.

When to Use

Use for any long-running service an orchestrator manages — web services, workers, agents behind a scheduler or platform that probes health.

Do not run side effects in probes; a health check that writes, rotates, or caches changes system state on a timer nobody scheduled.

Inputs

Procedure
Implement two endpoints: liveness reports process health from in-process state only; readiness reports the ability to serve.
Make readiness walk the real dependencies with short timeouts; a dependency down means unready, not a restart.
Keep checks cheap and side-effect free — probing sits on the request path of every scheduling decision.
Tune probe intervals and thresholds above the noise floor; flapping thresholds convert blips into restart storms.
Degrade to unready under partial dependency failure, and report which dependency held the gate.
Log state transitions with the reason; restart and no-traffic events are only debuggable with that record.

Outputs

Runnable Example

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

Health endpoints report process state; they do not validate data quality, security posture, or business correctness. Those belong to monitoring, security scanning, and SLOs — separate signals with separate owners.

Kubernetes Deployment

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

A Deployment manifest is where container defaults become incidents: floating tags, unset resource bounds, identical probes, and an implicit rollout strategy. This skill defines the manifest contract: pin the image, declare requests and limits, give readiness and liveness probes distinct purposes, and state the rollout strategy and history bound explicitly.

Use when authoring or reviewing a Kubernetes Deployment manifest for a long-running service.

Do not use for one-off pods, batch Jobs, or StatefulSets; their lifecycle contracts differ and need their own manifests.

Pin the image to an immutable tag or digest; latest is not a deployable version.
Declare resource requests and limits for every container; unbounded containers share fate with their neighbors.
Give readiness and liveness probes different purposes and settings; identical probes detect nothing distinct.
Set the replica count and the rollout strategy explicitly, including max unavailable and max surge.
Configure a bounded revision history so rollback targets exist without growing forever.

Validate the manifest with a dry run before applying; schema errors belong in review, not in apply output.
Record the deploy outcome, including revision, conditions, and observed replicas, and compare against the declared intent.

Select the distribution strategy deliberately; affinity only with an application reason.
Configure health checks with thresholds tuned to fail toward removing a backend.
Set connection limits sized to the weakest backend, not the strongest.

title: Secrets Management
description: Store and deliver credentials through a managed system — never in code or config files — with scoped leases, rotation, and audit, so a leak has a blast radius and an end date.
body:
Secrets Management

Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1

Description

A credential in a config file is a credential in a repository, a backup, and a log shipper forever. This skill routes around that: secrets live in a dedicated store, workloads fetch them at start time under an authenticated identity, each credential carries a scope and a lease, and rotation is routine rather than an incident. The audit trail closes the loop — who fetched what, when, under which role — because the question after a leak is never only what got out, but what it could reach and for how long.

When to Use

Use for any credential a workload needs — API keys, database credentials, signing material — delivered at runtime by identity, with rotation intervals that limit the lifetime of a stolen value.

Do not build home-grown encryption schemes or stash credentials in environment files that outlive their leak; the managed path exists precisely so the shortcuts do not have to.

Inputs

Procedure
Inventory the credentials first: every secret gets an owner, a scope, and a rotation interval before it gets a store entry.
Store values only in the secrets system, addressed by logical name, with no copies in code, config files, or CI variables.
Deliver at runtime: the workload authenticates as itself and receives only the entries its scope allows.
Lease and rotate: credentials expire by policy, and rotation is a routine operation with a tested procedure, not an emergency.
Audit every fetch — identity, secret, time — and route the log somewhere a compromised workload cannot edit.
Revoke on suspicion, and drill revocation like backups: a rotation path never exercised will fail exactly when it matters.

Outputs

Failure Modes

Security and Authority Boundary

The secrets system is the highest-value target in the estate: its stores must be encrypted at rest, its access decisions must run on workload identity rather than shareable credentials, and its audit logs must live outside the reach of the identities they record.
